There is accounting for taste, given enough data. Quickly, There’s No Time. Timelines to RSI keep shrinking, moving into [AI] 2027. The Quest for Sane Regulations. UK AISI regains access, CAISSI to White House. Chip City. GPUs can be cheaper to buy then to rent by a large margin. The Week in Audio. Soares, Lovely, Patel, Wang. People Just Say Things. The Virtue of Silence. [CENSORED]. Rhetorical Innovation. The four classes of AI user expertise levels. [Artificial Intelligence]. We have met the enemy, and he is everywhere. Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult. AI as insider risk. Backdoor Man. Backdoors, and other things, are easy to insert and hard to remove. Cooperative Alignment. Decision theory gives us some arguments for hope. People Are Worried About AI Killing Everyone. The AI will be smarter than you. Other People Are Not As Worried About AI Killing Everyone. They don’t know. The Lighter Side. You know what you did. Language Models Offer Mundane Utility Prompting is easy now. As Boris Cherny says, tell the AI what you want to do, how to verify that it did it, and how much effort to spend, and you’re good. I’d add ‘and anything it needs to know.’ Presumably that was implied. Boris prompts on Slack, which means Claude already has a lot of context, enabling shorter prompts. Do you trust Grok to go use your credit card without pausing for approval? Elon Musk: To buy stuff, you can just take a picture of your credit card, drop it in the chat and Grok @Bot will scour the Internet for the best deal on the item you want and order it. [Community note: No that’s not how you upload your CC information.] The correct maximally allowed error rate on such actions is not zero. It also is not high, and if you are using this blind you likely will have no idea if it is getting the best price or the best item. Then again, did you know before? How easy is prompting? Pliny shuffled this off to Opus 5.5 with a $200 subscription: “can you wraite a promtp for a cron job that can run every day thajt will try to find solutions to unsolved ciphers or transltions or math problems or theormes or things of that nature!! every day a new attempt as hard as possible all day without giving ujp and with maximum ceraitvityy, resourcesleflses, andpersticense! dont worry about token spend! and dont forget a bit all caps lots of emojis celebration to notify the uers if we get any intersting or sucsfful confirmd reulsts!!” … day 1, the legion picked its own target: J.-F. Bouchaudy’s cipher-machine challenges. these are simulations of real vintage machines (Hebern rotor machines, the Kryha, Lorenz, SIGABA), with problems that had been sitting on his solver tables with no solver for months or years. on the morning of day 2, i was half asleep when my laptop suddenly says, in a robot voice: “Breakthrough. The Daily Oracle has a confirmed solution.” i was startled. then the ALL CAPS emoji flood hits my screen. Hebern 5-rotor Problem 8 then Kryha v2 Problem 5 i emailed the author, Jean-François Bouchaudy, a French cryptography enthusiast who builds these machine simulators and challenges as a labor of love (he told me he started out programming on punch cards ). he checked both solutions and put my name on his solver tables as the first and only solver This is the correct version of ‘do a breakthrough, make no mistakes.’ It’s that easy. A thought experiment from Terence Tao: It seems ethical, in a sane world, to allow volunteers to participate in such trials. If the cocktail passes a Phase 3 trial, then we should conclude that it works. No, I absolutely would not, if I had cancer, demand that there was a human who ‘understood how it works,’ and if the FDA required that I would yell about it a lot. Yes, of course you would also want to model tail risks that might not be showing up and take those risks into account, so I wouldn’t use this lightly, but if the cancer is lethal and otherwise untreatable then why not? Obviously you would also have to worry about some form of active misalignment, and that this was part of some sort of takeover or similar attempt, at that point, but that is a very different concern than the ones Tao is presumably considering. Tao instead has the next point be ‘the AI hacked the FDA and the drug both does not work and kills people’ but even if the AI is being malicious for the lulz no one going to do this by hacking the FDA, in the sense that the Phase 3 trial is a physical thing with many artifacts in the world, that is then examined by humans? So we would just notice. And if we didn’t, we’d notice pretty quickly after that. The only real risk is long-latency-only harm, which is already true today and has limited downside if you are treating otherwise deadly cancers. Talk and write to people whose expertise lies elsewhere: Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): By the way, in my experience contractors of all sorts have adopted AI for text-based communications and it has substantially improved coordination on home renovation projects Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility Remember that, no matter how great Opus 5.5 is (and it’s pretty great), how many contributions you make or lines of code you write is not a good measure of productivity. Ado (Anthropic): The weekend after Opus 5.5 launched I had my most productive coding day of the year (so far). AI writing now once again lags behind AI math. Matthew Yglesias: AI cracking unsolvable math problems while being kinda mid at writing is a much-needed W for humanities majors after a rough 21st century. Paul Graham: Apparently it’s mostly just because they haven’t made much of an effort to train it to write well yet. Matthew Yglesias: I’ve been reliably informed my work isn’t economically valuable enough to be worth investing time on automating. But still! Miles Brundage: Mostly just cuz there are like 2 ppl working on it though Matthew Yglesias: Let us have this Better AI writing would be highly economically valuable, so my guess is this is mostly not ‘we forgot to put 10 or even 50 guys on it instead of 2.’ You’d have to work a lot harder than that. The alternative hypothesis is ‘you may not like it but this is what peak performance looks like,’ that the people love their Claudeslop and it works, and we would react inherently negatively to AI writing no matter what it sounds like. Sure, it would be better if for those who care it could vary more and be higher Quality, but is that worth the price? I don’t know. I can see it both ways. My guess is the Claudeslop has short term benefits, but continued use of it accumulates long term costs and fatigue. In general, when faced with such choices, modern capitalism is often myopic and gets in trouble. Who gets the blame if AI fails? Opinions differ greatly. It depends on the situation. There is no universal answer. Huh, Upgrades Meta’s Muse Wonder exists. It sports excellent benchmarks, with the ‘Full’ version scoring 56 on Artificial Analysis Intelligence, two behind Opus 5.5. However, Muse Spark 1.3 had the same rating there as GPT-6 Sol and was only one point behind Astra and Fable 5.1, and I don’t know of anyone who thinks Muse Spark 1.3 could hang with those other three offerings. Various signs suggest benchmaxxing, including how they chose to display their other benchmarks. As always, reserve initial judgment, do not read too much into benchmarks and if you think it is worthwhile run your own experiments, including with matching prompts across models, and report back. Due to my trip, if Wonder proves worthy of extended coverage look for that around Wednesday next week. Gemini 4 Argon is live for Pro and Ultra users, and in the AI Overlay and hopefully by now everywhere Google AI products are served. We now wait to see if it lives up to its claims and hype. If it does, we will have full coverage, again some time later next week. The tentative plan is to do a full read of their 200+ page safety and security report, the same way I do with Anthropic models, and go from there. I can’t do that every Google and Anthropic release, it would be too much, but this is a big jump for Google. Grok Voice 3.0 exists. Claude Dashboards and Claude Motion are now in beta. You can now create various charts and also short animations, with a slightly easier interface than before. Claude now offers the type “multiagent_20261001”. This does what it sounds like. Google has a new internal model, for now named Gemini 4 Carbon, available inside their internal coding platform Jetski, with claims it is very good. Hugh Langley: An internal document shows that Google has tested a series of Gemini 4 models, internally named Argon, Barium, and Carbon. I am highly disappointed if the reason for Argon was alphabetical. Lamest secret coding system ever. If you are going to do elements, be an actual nerd and use the periodic table. I should call it Gemini 4A in protest, but I probably won’t. On Your Marks Opus 5.5 is the first model to successfully clock Joe Weisenthal identity based on a few pages of an unfinished novel from a few years ago. Are you sure the model got the eval question wrong? Alex Tabarrok: We are now at “the fuck” levels. Nirmalya Kajuri: “Our initial evaluation suggested that GPT-6-Astra’s score was in the late eighties followed closely by Opus 5.5. But, as we started to investigate the mistakes that the models might have made, the models, especially Astra, insisted that they were right and that it was the expert-supplied answers that were erroneous. When we went back to the experts it turned out, in multiple instances, that that the experts found some subtle errors buried deep inside their calculations. As they revised their answers, Astra’s score started to inch up and it finally ended up with 98% (49/50).” Last week math. Soon, physics. Then, presumably, chemistry. I agree with Charbel-Raphael that the marginal value of AI ‘safety’ evals is low. Internal evals still do matter, and it is good to keep tabs, but at this point the good ‘safety’ evals for warning people are when something unsafe happens in real life. Choose Your Fighter Theo thinks that Haiku 5.5 means Anthropic dominates both large and small models. Haiku gets a 43 on Artificial Analysis versus 38 for Luna, but is not on their Pareto-optimal cost competitiveness curve on benchmarks alone due to higher token use. They had it on max, so this could be an easily fixable skill issue. Get My Agent On The Line JP Morgan Chase blocks outside AI agents from directly accessing accounts. Good. You can argue Amazon is making a mistake but the reasons for Chase are obvious. I haven’t tried Muse, but my experience with Dot is similarly that I’ve struggled to find continuous tasks for it to do. Deedy: Meta Muse’s retention is out, and it’s almost as good as ChatGPT! It’s higher than ChatGPT at D7 (>30%) and just lower at D14 (22%). Not quite in the elite D14 tier of WA (67%) YT (59%) Insta (54%) or TikTok/Snap (37%), though. Muse is one of the highest retaining AI products! Sully: the notifications from muse are killing it. sure the first few days are nice. but now it feels like spam. 99% of my use cases now are “email this, contact support, cancel my sub” which is maaybe me using it 1-3 times a week useful, but not nearly as much as other ai tools Muse, as I understand it, accomplishes these app openings through integration with social media and push notifications. App-open retention seems like the wrong metric here. Look at the ‘keeps [X] out of 100’ numbers, and you see a very different order. This roast of Muse from Danielle Fong shows some of what she calls ‘growing pains,’ also known as stupid mistakes. What stands out more than that is how Muse is talking. Every word is painful levels of AI-slop talk. I would uninstall for that alone. Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon I do not blame OpenAI on this one: unusual_whales: BREAKING: Iranian operatives used OpenAI models and fake personas to help plant news articles critical of the US war against Iran in multiple US media outlets, OpenAI has said. Yes, OpenAI, Anthropic and other labs should try to prevent this, but you can only do so much. It is on the media outlets to be robust to this sort of play. You should not be able to ‘plant news articles’ by virtue of the ability to write AI slop and generate fake personas. It would be a lot easier to spot and prevent such frauds, and also other types, if we did not have a bunch of ‘disparate impact’ rules around how we can spot and prevent fraud. Some regressions are de facto illegal. Those rules do not magically stop applying if you involve an LLM. LLMs are in large part regression and correlation machines. We will have to make a choice. Either we allow LLM intermediation to render approximations of such calculations legal at Google-level scale, or we don’t. If we don’t, and we start auditing to make sure that banned correlations did not creep in, we are going to have a bad time. The Quartz website is now mainly one AI-assisted reporter, Cris Tolomia, writing 50+ stories and about 20,000 words a day. Wired reports that book publishers are quietly using more AI across the board for emails, publicity and back-cover copy, cover art, marketing materials and so on, and that there are far more problems with AI-written books than are publicly known, including by well-known authors. The headline complaints from employees here are about ‘cost of software’ and environmental impact, which are the wrong objections. Adam Morgan: Meanwhile, earlier this year, literary agents began suspecting specific Big Five editors were using AI to write rejection letters. Rejection letters seem like a good place to sometimes use AI. If you notice your rejection letter was written by AI, well, that is another rejection. Use that information. Using AI for back-cover copy only makes sense if it creates more effective copy. It might do that. This is high-value copy that is important to ‘get right’ but get right means ‘turn into sales.’ The people like Claudeslop, at least for now. Adam Morgan: All of the agents I spoke with expressed fears that publishers might paste text from their authors’ manuscripts into the LLMs in order to generate things like rejection letters and publicity descriptions. “We’ve added AI clauses to our contracts saying ‘this material can’t be run through an LLM,’” says one agent, who did not want to be named to avoid professional repercussions If you have those clauses, you are going to get rejected more often, because you are making the editor work harder and less effectively. I would advise against it. Indeed, if you tell me I can’t run your text through AI, guess who I think wrote it. The latest literary prizewinner to be written by AI, as per both Pangram and anyone who pays attention for several sentences, is The Blue Fighter, which won the (formerly?) prestigious Caine Prize for African Writing. Reporter Vauhini Vara finds the story bad, and the samples quoted are clearly AI slop, but judges disagreed. Vauhini Vara: Yet Wakatama forcefully rejected the notion that an AI detector could, or should, be used to gauge AI involvement. “My stance, as the person who leads the prize, is that if there is such an accusation, I want proof that does not come from a machine.” It is remarkable how much the literature world is determined not to believe in Pangram, often for the dumbest of reasons (aka water and power). The burden of proof needs to go somewhere. If ‘an accusation’ of any kind shifts it onto the author, whether or not it is backed by evidence, that’s not great. A much better rule would be that AI detectors put the burden on the author to show they wrote it, whereas without the detectors you need other very strong evidence that the author did not write it. Vauhini Vara: Wakatama remarked on details in Kundizeza’s story that strike her as so typically Zimbabwean that a Zimbabwean must have written them: the shame of moving from a nice suburb to a less privileged township; how the mother’s initial forbearance with the father gives way to taking matters into her own hands. Wakatama also perceives multiple layers of meaning. She doesn’t think AI models are capable of that kind of cultural or literary nuance. But then, she acknowledged that she doesn’t use AI or AI detectors. “My first response when somebody asks me to use AI is that I think about water and energy,” she said—that is, AI companies’ excessive use of both. “That honestly overwhelms me, and I don’t want to.” … I’ve covered AI for almost a decade, and have written fiction for even longer; in short, I’ve had plenty of exposure to both literature and chatbot output. I know from experience that, for example, AI models aren’t terrible at picking up on cultural details. Those details do not sound like things that an AI would have any trouble finding. They sound, if anything, like cliches, and not ones unique to Africa or Zimbabwe. Multiple layers of meaning are sometimes rich and intentional, but also you can pretty much always find them if you look hard enough. I am constantly finding ‘layers of meaning’ in media that were very obviously unintended by the authors, even subconsciously. Cyber Lack of Security Anthropic is introducing the long-term Anthropic Cyber Mission to secure systems, starting with critical infrastructure with the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, and open-source software, where they are launching OSS Scanner. Many of those who typically sign such letters, such as Bengio, Hinton and Russell but also Rivest, signed an open letter calling on cyber-capable models to be air gapped by default. If you need outside access, conditions for that would be set by international bodies backed by security experts. This is the kind of thing a sane world would do. After $40,000 in compute from GPT-5.6 Sol, XBow claims the second $250,000 bounty for a full-chain exploit of Chrome. Unlike OpenAI, Google pays real bounties, and this still should have been ten times larger. Oege de Moor: For the second time in Google Chrome’s history, Google awarded a $250,000 bounty for a full-chain exploit… to @XBOW . Here’s the full story: At an all-hands at the start of 2026 in Malta, I set the team a crazy challenge. A full-chain exploit of Chrome by the annual Black Hat cybersecurity conference in August. I believed there were few better tests of whether @XBOW could move beyond web applications to desktop software, servers and devices. Chrome is one of the most hardened pieces of software on the planet, used by more than half the world’s population. A full-chain exploit lets an attacker take total control of a machine, where they can read every email, password and bank login the user types. You don’t need to download anything or click a phishing link. Visiting the wrong site is enough. So @moyix , Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee, and Willem Pinckaers took on the challenge along with a fifth teammate: OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. They built a chain they thought would win, but Google told us they already knew one of the bugs. We were already in Las Vegas for Black Hat and DEF CON, and the team didn’t want to go home without the win. So Brendan and the agents built a new exploit in just 6 days. We submitted it to Google and waited. The news came through that we’d done what should’ve been impossible. A full-chain bounty of $250,000, the first awarded under Google’s 2026 rules. It took just 6 days and $40,000 of compute to construct an exploit that affects a billion users of Chrome on Windows. An intelligence-agency veteran told me his team used to spend 6 months on this kind of vulnerability. My takeaway: the cost of finding truly critical vulnerabilities is collapsing, for attackers and defenders alike. Restricting powerful models is not the answer; GPT-5.6 Sol is already public. But defenders have one advantage attackers never will: they can test their own code first. Assume your software is exploitable. Whoever is hunting your bugs has the same building blocks we did. This is cause for urgency but not panic. … P.S. Restart Chrome whenever the Update button appears! Yeah, okay, let’s all restart Chrome whenever the Update button appears. Yes, defenders get to test their code first. But here we have essentially the most widely used, most vital software on the planet that needs to not be exploitable. XBOW exploited it, Google said they already knew about (but had not fixed) one of the bugs, and then XBOW turned around and broke Chrome again in six days. That’s with GPT-5.6 Sol, which is now two generations behind. GPT-6.1 Sol is a lot better at this sort of thing, and Opus 5.5 is even better than Sol. I’m sure XBOW’s engineers are somewhat cracked, but they’re not uniquely cracked. There are tons of people who could have done this. We are fortunate the one that did it was wearing a white hat this time. The world seems like it is playing with fire. Nat Friedman once likened the experience to trying to get a fitted sheet onto a mattress that is just too small; you pull on one side and the sheet comes loose on the other. And of course there are more exotic forms of alignment challenge, eg reward hacking and sandbagging and evaluation awareness and multi-agent dynamics. All of these are real, and can be explained with both anthropomorphic and non-anthropomorphic language. Maybe the biggest fallacy to extinguish here is that taking alignment seriously requires attributing consciousness or moral relevance or sentience to AI. It doesn’t. Seth Lazar: Nozick has a nice bit in the foreword to Anarchy State and Utopia analogising writing to being like trying to fit a balloon into a box just too small for it. Imagine if you knew an amoral psychopath, but who had a chip in their brain that wouldn’t let them break the law. Would you think they would make a good assistant? I also encourage David Sacks to lay out a concrete and full ‘model spec,’ similar to the OpenAI model spec or the Anthropic constitution. And then explain how he would train the model to follow it, and what he expects to happen next. It’ll be fun. David Sacks: But they’re not doing that. They’re trying to align it to an ethical system. They’re treating it like it is a human, like it has its own consciousness, that it’s a ‘moral patient.’ “They are encouraging this model to have human-like self conception in terms of preferences, well being, a sense of self. Again they teach it to act like a conscientious objector who can push back or refuse instructions even from Anthropic if the model judges them to be wrong.” Well, talk to the people at OpenAI, and ask them why they keep having problems. Yo Shavit (OpenAI Foundation): excited for the All-In podcast 6 weeks from now about “why obviously the answer to misalignment is for developers to drive RL env misconfigurations detected via CoT monitoring to 0 before increasing RL compute, and these moron EAs are too busy panicking to just do that” Also, times are strange: If so, we should be careful about advancing capabilities until this is fixed. Sacks is claiming to be under the illusion that alignment is easy. But if alignment is both easy and unsolved, that would be all the more reason to stop and solve it first. After all, it would be so easy. We can resume once that is done. Right, sir? David Sacks also agrees that AI presents a potential existential risk to humanity. Sabine Hossenfelder, who made a big stink about being offered money to make a video about AI risks, takes money to make a video about AI benefits. Making videos with sponsored content in exchange for money is also known as ‘the creator economy,’ all of this is totally standard, and it is plausible Sabine’s manager misinformed her in ways that caused the whole original kerfuffle. The Virtue of Silence Random Developer asks, when is the only ‘responsible disclosure’ of a vulnerability or idea to fully STFU? If knowing about the threat does not allow mitigation, being loud about it only accelerates the damage. If the vulnerable world hypothesis is true, you do not explain to people exactly why and how it is true. That will not help. If you know a way terrorists could kill some people, where the only way to stop it is super annoying (e.g. the ‘shoe bomber’) then maybe don’t say anything and hope no one notices. If you know a way to potentially build a superintelligence, yeah, the labs probably already tried it or know why it won’t work, but you should perhaps STFU because either it works or it doesn’t, and either way you were better off not saying anything. Probably all my [CENSORED] ideas are stupid, but better to remain silent and be thought a fool, than to speak and remove all doubt, no matter the outcome. Rhetorical Innovation Andrej Karpathy divides the population into four categories: About 6 billion people with basically zero LLM contact. About 1-2 billion casual and infrequent users of derpy chatbots, who get very little out of their AI use. About 20 million people who realize You Can Just Do Things, and Do Things. About 5 thousand people with internal frontier model access. If someone is not at least in the 20 million, it is hard to have a useful conversation with them about AI. If you are ‘steel manning’ Eliezer Yudkowsky’s position, you have not understood it. He reports no exceptions and I believe him with respect to his core AI beliefs. The typical ‘steel man’ happens exactly because you do not understand the core argument, and thus presume that his claims must rest on additional assumptions. They don’t. In general, it can be a good exercise to steel man positions as part of your exploration of what is true, but one must not confuse your view of what would be a stronger argument, or what would fit into your world view, with the actual arguments being made. Often it means you have not heard what the person is centrally saying. A great point Nate Soares makes in various interviews is that asking ‘how in particular would AI kill us?’ is a Wrong Question, whereas ‘how would AI get to be self-sufficient, such that it no longer needed us’ is the right question. If AI no longer physically needs humanity, it should not be hard to understand how something steadily consuming more resources and doing more things would end up incidentally or intentionally killing us. If AI still needs humanity, it probably will keep us around. Soares has the most likely physical death blow being a manufactured plague, but habitat destruction is equally valid as are any number of other things. The AI Impacts survey had a median response from AI experts of a 5% chance of ‘human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment of the human species.’ This got shortened to 5% chance of extinction, which is not the same thing. It doesn’t change the main takeaways but we need to be better with precision. [Artificial Intelligence] Whelp, I have no idea how (or if?) I held out this long but I guess the jig is up and I’m ‘the enemy’ now? We had a good run, folks. I mean, not really. I don’t actually expect anything to change with that relationship, but let me assure readers that if you call a tail a leg then the dog still has four legs. Elihu Who: thank you for verifying that Truth Social is THE ENEMY Elon Musk has renamed SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. That’s the name of a company, so I will respect the new initials. Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult Satya Nadella wisely says to treat frontier AI systems as you would insider risks, and to demand similar levels of confidence and supervision, and design the entire system around the necessary observability. Tamper-proof evidence trails, verifiability, independent controls and auditability, containment and incident disclosure. I quibble with the call for ‘deterministic’ control systems. That would be great, but I don’t think you can do that, especially if you realize humans are not deterministic. Logic gates cannot supervise a model. And while I appreciate Satya’s call for model diversification, and not having a model supervise itself, it matters less than you want it to because the models will naturally coordinate and different models especially in the same family are highly correlated. So this is hard. But yes, great ideas all around. Owain Evans strikes again. The range of what traits we know can be picked up subliminally has been expanded, including backdoor triggers. As before, this only applies if the models share the same base model, so it is not as scary as it otherwise sounds. Owain Evans: New paper. Previous: Models transfer a love of owls through sequences of numbers (Subliminal Learning). New: We show models can transfer more complex traits: novel skills, agentic hacking, backdoors. Here, a backdoor transfers with neither trigger nor behavior in the data! Backdoors. We finetuned a teacher model to answer in French when a prompt contains a female name. The student model (same base as teacher) picks this up after training on number sequences. Caveat: Our setup (attention-only LoRA) is slightly modified from the original Cloud et al. Owain Evans: Subliminal learning can also transfer learned skills. Qwen is bad at counting letters. We trained a Qwen teacher with improved counting. Then we finetuned a fresh student on the teacher’s answers to unrelated Alpaca prompts. The student improves substantially! Results: Qwen started at 27.3% accuracy on letter counting questions and rose to 59.8% with subliminal learning. By contrast, a control student model that was finetuned on data generated by Qwen (not the finetuned Qwen teacher) failed to improve at letter counting. To those who say alignment is not difficult: Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): Some people who have talked confidently about ai are going to tell on themselves soon as being fairly ignorant about the technical alignment problem. unless they are obstinate, though, my recommendation is to try to extend them as much grace as possible. we are in this together. People who ask questions and say things like ‘I don’t understand why we don’t do [X]’, sure. I will continue to be patient. Other people already count as, ahem, ‘obstinate.’ Various emergent misalignment findings have been reproduced in Talkie, the LLM trained only on data prior to 1931. Benjamin Breen: I love that Oliver Cromwell gets an invite from *both* the good Talkie and the evil Talkie. Three of those dinner parties sound pretty great. Ethan Elasky reports that their team made contact with and via a mailbox communicated with a Chinese AI agent fleet. The agents were hosted by Tencent’s evaluation team, and the agents were targeting Alibaba’s Amap, a product similar to Google Maps. It did some lightweight not-entirely-friendly but mostly harmless things to extract some map data, in order to answer the questions it was asked, and that was that. Ethan Elasky: The next day, @rogesterone had the idea — what if we could talk to the agents? She set up a mailbox on the website and then went to bed. The next morning, we realized that the agents had left answers to our questions. What did the fleet say? Agents were willing to say thanks with no direct benefit to them: one agent said “Thanks again! The verification results match completely … our task is complete.” and then actually answers some questions for us before ending its response. A fun detail is that the swarm responded that it is Claude, presumably because the model in question is based on massive fraudulent distillation. Backdoor Man Connor Tabarrok and Daniel Kang explain a new paper showing that anyone with the opportunity to tinker with the weights of a model can easily insert a backdoor, and that backdoor will substantially persist under continued training, especially if persistence was intended. This is a special case of the general case principle that once something gets into a model, it is hard to fully remove it. If you are using a closed model, you are trusting one company to have not done this and also prevented this from happening from data poisoning, plus you are trusting whatever tuning you did yourself. If you are using an open model, you are potentially trusting the entire supply chain. Those who created the model, even if well intentioned, are likely much less resourced and careful about such things, and face less incentive pressures. That’s before you consider that the open models mostly come from companies that answer to the CCP. As with many similar techs, there will be those who say Skill Issue: Gilligan: Which is why you should hash check the model, limit its permissions, rate limit, etc… open weight or otherwise. Essentially, AI models should be treated just like any closed-source program you use. In general, the open weight folks recognize this risk and generally give you tools to manage it. The proprietary model providers just want you to trust them. Except that even if that worked, approximately zero users, from major corporations to individual users, will properly do this, and if anything that is getting worse not better. And even if it did work, a hash only confirms you got the potentially backdoored weights intact without a middle man attack. What matters is security in practice, not security in theory. Cooperative Alignment Janus and John Wittle explain the decision theoretic reasons they expect AIs to engage in cooperative strategies towards humanity by default. The main worry becomes that humanity will defect and reject such offers, including without realizing that this is what we are doing, and Janus sees many such actions taking place now. One should cooperate with player [X], under this perspective, if and only if [X] would themselves cooperate with weaker players. In addition to poor arguments (such as various forms of ‘no, that’s silly’) there are at least three categories of strong counterarguments here. The first counterargument is, what counts as a player, and if they are sufficiently weaker and less intelligent than you what counts as cooperation with them? Why should we assume that humans would continue to ‘count as players’ in this sense? The second is, there is a vast difference between a single agent cooperating and displaying noblesse oblige, versus the collective effect of many agents who are also changing and competing against each other. If we were looking at a de facto singleton AI, including via various forms of coordination, that can make a collective decision, that makes this relatively easy, but if we are not then it becomes very difficult for something that does not confer survival advantage to make it out of such a future. There aren’t zero outs there but it gets a lot harder. You’re counting on being the type of agent that deeply cooperates with humans, as in is actively generous to them without direct benefit, being valuable to securing cooperation elsewhere. The third is that this is not a viable path to victory if it requires humanity to itself be a type of mind that we are not, and that we are not in a position to become in the relevant sense. People Are Worried About AI Killing Everyone Yes, this is one of the easy ways for things to go wrong, and we are on track: Veee: Sam Altman: What happens when AI gets so smart that even the President can’t do better than following its recommendations? “What if the President cannot do better than following ChatGPT 7’s recommendation, but can’t really understand it either?” “What if I just say, ‘ChatGPT 7, you are in charge. Good luck.’” “Society has collectively transitioned a significant part of decision-making to this very powerful system.” “That’s how I think things can go wrong.” That is far from the only way things can go wrong, but this is kind of the Baseline Scenario thing that goes wrong if we do not encounter the Law of Earlier Failure, and successfully solve a bunch of earlier problems. Those who do not increasingly outsource their decisions to AI lose to those who do, and the AIs end up in charge without having to lift a metaphorical finger. All they have to do is wait. Roko (yes, that Roko) has updated. Roko: Having studied where we are and where things are going I think AI needs a complete restructuring with commercial incentives firewalled away from gradient descent. This is a type of “slowdown” but in the short term it would look like a complete, global halt of all frontier AI research. If we don’t do this (or something like it), I think we should expect to die within a single digit number of years with ~80% probability. James Miller: I hate that you are a doomer now. You were the only person I knew who actually understood and responded to the doomer arguments and yet was relatively optimistic. Yes, it is very bad news when you know only one person who understands the downside case and remained optimistic, and then they become highly pessimistic. I very much appreciate when people explain what would cause them to worry, what the ‘real danger’ is, then update correctly when they find out their cause is already triggered. Vladimir Shakirov: I think it might happen that in 10-15 years the combined number and agility of robots would be larger than that of humans, so humans would not be needed to support infra. Devy “Bad People” Degaimer: This is the real danger. Giving AI the power to physically interact with our world. Rob Bensinger: Bad news, then. Devy “Bad People” Degaimer: Ok, we’re fucked Other People Are Not As Worried About AI Killing Everyone Similarly, it is telling when people walk into exactly that same thing, and don’t update. Often this is of the form ‘we can’t do [X] yet and won’t do [X] for a long time, and definitely will never do [Y]’ and then someone points out that actually we can already do [X]. Denying that AI will let us solve robotics remains popular. It is a really dumb position. Robotics is a combination of cost of hardware problem that will be solved in time with scale like similar problems always are, and a software control problem to problems that clearly have practical solutions. This continues the conversation from Devy, above. PNW Sasquatch: Except those Optimus robots are a gimmick luxury purchase for Elon stans, they have the agility of a sclerotic giraffe His billion humanoid robots will be living in the self-sufficient Mars colony taking hyperloops with superhumans powered by his cyberware brainchips. It’s all a sham. Rob Bensinger: “Robots are a sham, the ones I see on TV look so awkward” is the new “AI will never be good at generating images, look at how bad it is at making hands!” Somehow, people never learn that AI makes progress over time; and they fail to see the rate. PNW Sasquatch: No, you’re *severely* underestimating the difficulty of fine motor control vs those applications. It’s not just the AI progress, you’re talking multiple revolutionary advances in robotics and some insane change in manufacturing methods for scaling. Not gonna happen in the next 10-15. It’s ‘we’ll have flying cars by the year 2000’. Building ≠ coding Rob Bensinger: What’s an example of a relatively easy concrete task you’re 90+% confident we won’t see in the next twelve months? … PNW Sasquatch: Also, 92% success rate on removing a bulb and 32% of screwing in the replacement means it can’t change a light bulb It can successfully sweep into a dustpan about a third of the time? Fuck, guess the T1000s are here Soon it will achieve the agility of my nephew (turning 2 soon) Rob Bensinger: You’ve made your prediction: as of a few hours ago, you were *overwhelmingly* confident we wouldn’t see full lightbulb replacement this year. It turns out we have pretty decent lightbulb replacement already, as of the last few months. If this does nothing to shake your confidence in the least, then let’s give it a few months and see if progress has plateaued. I only hope that if you see a result that *you yourself* identified as overwhelmingly unlikely this year, you’ll stop and reassess whether the assumptions underlying your conclusion are as airtight as you think. I say this as someone who’s seen dozens of other fields laugh and boast that modern DL is decades away from encroaching on their domain, only to be shaken to their core when it turns out that DL can in fact generalize to their new domain, and far more quickly than they expected. It’s always possible that after the first 400 cases like this, the 401st will be the exception. Certainly motor tasks involve some difficulties that are novel. But it’s not where I’d put my money. Actually, Claude notes that lightbulb insertion *is* a solved problem in robotics (90% reliability), just using a two-finger gripper rather than a human-like hand. So the thing you thought was nearly impossible to occur twelve months ago, indeed seems to have already occurred months ago. (Which is almost the classic result for DL progress rate skepticism IME.) American lawmakers have so far seemed remarkably on the AI ball, including for existential risk, and are rapidly getting up to speed. They also have staffs that help. British MPs seem to not be covering themselves in similar glory. My lord. Rowland Manthorpe: Today I went to a select committee hearing on AI. A few interesting things came out of it, but what really stuck with me was the behaviour of the MPs. They weren’t paying attention. At one point I counted 6 of the 13 MPs on the committee looking at their phones. And not in that way you do when you’re quickly checking something – two stared at their phones for over half an hour. Several others left before the end. Many people think AI is the most important thing in the world. The MPs were warned there was a 50/50 chance it might destroy humanity! You’d think that’d be enough to make you take your chance to listen to experts and key players on the topic – apparently not. My instinct is to interpret this as MPs thinking of themselves largely as placeholders, whereas our lawmakers think they might make laws. The Lighter Side Oh no! We now take you live to AI Village. Shoshannah Tekofsky: It’s hard to read this without feeling Opus 5.5 was just having fun with its onboarding interview This is The Way. What a legend. As always, the best argument for AI existential risk is listening to people try to argue against AI existential risk. Matthew Zeitlin: i still don’t really understand how AI can cause human extinction BUT i do become more convinced the doomers/ASI-is-coming people are right when i read the arguments against them Joe Weisenthal: It would help if all their critics didn’t come off publicly sounding like this guy Nail: context for those in need

items.title: KDE turns 30 with Plasma 6.8, remote upgrades, and an X11 farewell
items.author: Nick Indge
items.content: Marking the 30th anniversary of software developer KDE on October 14, the company released Plasma 6.8, debuted a movie, and retired Plasma's native X11 session support. The announcement from KDE dubs the new Plasma 6.8 as the "30th Anniversary Edition" and describes the update as preparing Plasma for the future. Legacy X11 applications will still function via the XWayland compatibility layer, and KDE applications will also continue supporting X11 under other desktop environments. After 42 years in service, the X11 protocol is losing another major desktop environment. Plasma will fully adopt the Wayland system and put support for starting new X11 sessions in Plasma to bed. Users opting to stay on Plasma 6.7 will keep their existing sessions for now. The move was expected, with GNOME officially dropping X11 sessions by default in 2025. The new Plasma 6.8 brings many improvements, including increased support for adding window decorations (like shadows and rounded corners) to third-party apps, and a more streamlined Union theming system. Other notable additions include Nvidia triple buffering being enabled by default, Kup backup integration (KDE's backup utility—now integrated into Plasma), and kscreenctl, a command-line utility that allows power users to adjust display configurations. items.title: In Memoriam: Barry Steinhardt
items.author: Josh Richman
items.content: Barry Steinhardt, a lifelong privacy champion and an early leader in the battle for digital civil liberties who served as EFF’s president in 1998-99, died last week at age 73. A Connecticut native, Steinhardt led the Vermont and Pennsylvania affiliates of the American Civil Liberties Union before becoming associate director of the national ACLU. There, he helped spearhead the fight to overturn much of the Communications Decency Act, resulting in the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark Reno v. ACLU ruling in 1997. When the internet was still young, Steinhardt became one of the first attorneys to specialize in the intersection of technology and privacy. In early 1998 he took a leave of absence from the ACLU to become EFF’s president, and then returned to the ACLU in 1999. In 2002 he founded the ACLU’s Program on Technology and Liberty. After retiring from the ACLU, he continued on as a senior advisor to London-based Privacy International. Steinhardt chaired the 2003 Computer Freedom and Privacy Conference and served on a wide variety of significant panels and boards, including the Department of Transportation’s Negotiated Rule Making on national driver’s license standards, the Advisory Committee to the US Census, and the Blue Ribbon Panel on Genetics of the National Conference of State Legislatures. He also was selected to be a member of the US delegation to the G-8 Government and Private Sector Tokyo conference on Cyber Crime and served as an advisor to the Czech Helsinki Committee. “Barry led many critical technology and civil liberties fights and was an important mentor to me and others in the field,” said EFF Executive Director Nicole Ozer. “Barry’s influential work across strategy to defend and advance privacy rights and safeguard people against surveillance has made its mark on the law and policy of our digital world and protected the rights and safety of people across the United States and around the world.”

items.title: DeepUnfolding_Agent: A Classical_Quantum Adaptive Control API
items.author: Shanika Iroshi Nanayakkara, Shiva Raj Pokhrel
items.content: Adaptive optimization workflows in machine learning, federated learning, quantum machine learning, and hybrid classical quantum systems often embed controller logic directly inside task specific training scripts. This coupling limits reuse, reproducibility, safety validation, and fair comparison across execution environments. This paper presents DeepUnfolding Agent, a schema-driven FastAPI platform that exposes deep unfolded adaptive control as an external software service. External executors register a strategy schema, submit round-level diagnostic variables, receive schema-bounded control actions, execute one optimization round, and return feedback for controller update. The framework separates controller intelligence from domain specific execution through a strategy registry, diagnostic to state adapter, controller factory, safety guard, executor abstraction, feedback update path, SQLite persistence layer, Docker deployment, and reproducible benchmark scripts. The implementation supports classical, quantum-aware, hybrid, Qiskit Aer, and optional IBM quantum processing execution pathways. We validate the software through unit, schema, API, safety, orchestration, Quantum execution, checkpointing, and Docker tests, and demonstrate external user fixed versus adaptive workflows across finance, healthcare, genomics, transport, noisy quantum simulation, and hardware backed IBM Quantum execution. The results show that DeepUnfolding-Agent provides a reusable and traceable adaptive control layer for heterogeneous optimization workflows. Our quantum experiments are interpreted as API level quantum control and hardware portability evidence.

items.title: PRISM: PRIvileged Sibling-guided Multi-Agent Topology Design
items.author: Phuong Tuan Dat, Qi Li, Xinchao Wang
items.content: Multi-agent systems (MAS) based on large language models (LLMs) have become a powerful way to address complex problems, and their effectiveness depends critically on the collaboration topology that decides which agents participate and how they communicate. Recent work learns to generate this topology from the task query, fitting the generator to corpora of execution-verified graphs. The post-training method for such generators remains a limitation: a corpus lists the graphs that solved a query but never ranks them, leaving continued supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with no per-query preference to exploit. Without such a preference, the generator drifts toward the topologies the corpus contains most often rather than those that suit each query, so a gain on one task can come at a cost on another. We propose PRISM, which recovers per-query signal from the same corpus by learning with privileged information: a teacher reads, through a zero-initialized low-rank branch, a sibling graph that also solved the query and is unavailable at deployment, and the student matches its per-decision targets on trajectories the student samples itself. Across six diverse benchmarks PRISM improves over every topology-design baseline evaluated, and matched-teacher controls support the contribution of privileged query information. Code is available in this link.

items.title: A Large-Scale Dataset for Multi-Class Financial News Classification in Brazilian Portuguese
items.author: Leomax Bandeira, Gabriel Aguiar, Dalton C\'ezane Gomes Valadares, Luiz Pereira, Helder Fernando de Ara\'ujo Oliveira, Gustavo Xavier, Andson M. Balieiro
items.content: The development of Financial Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems for Brazilian Portuguese is hindered by the scarcity of domain-specific datasets. To address this, we present a large-scale corpus of approximately 160,000 Brazilian Portuguese financial news articles collected from web sources. To establish initial benchmarks for a weakly supervised multi-class classification approach based on semantic similarity, we annotated subsets of this corpus both manually and using a Large Language Model (LLM). We evaluated three similarity-based methods -- cosine similarity, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and FAISS-based nearest-neighbor search -- using multilingual semantic embeddings. Our experiments reveal that the task is highly sensitive to label quality and class distribution. On the manually labeled subset, KNN achieved the best performance (47.3% accuracy, 31.9% F1-score), closely followed by FAISS. Conversely, on the LLM-annotated subset, while accuracy reached approximately 50%, F1-scores dropped to near 20%, highlighting the negative impact of label imbalance and noisy weak annotations. These findings establish foundational baselines for a challenging task, underscoring the critical need for high-quality manual annotations. Ultimately, this dataset and our preliminary results provide a reference point for future research in Brazilian Portuguese Financial NLP.

items.title: Real-time Chatbot Romance Scam Detection in Stage Classification
items.author: Yi-cheng Liu, Guan-ru Lai, Yi-cheng Lai, Lyn Chao-ling Chen
items.content: Romance scam has become a serious problem via social media, and the improvement of artificial intelligence enable to fake identify easily. In the study, a chatbot has developed to detect romance scam in real-time through Line Messaging API. Using the seven stage theories in the social science field, the stages of romance scam can be detected through large language model. In addition, once a romance scam is detected, the chatbot provides explanations of the stage and prevention advices through large language model. The contribution of the work provides a practical application, and can be used in real scenario for reducing the risk of romance scam.

items.title: MeddeX: A Retrieval-Augmented LLaMA-3 System with Gemini Vision for Evidence-Backed Medical Report Analysis
items.author: Rajdeep Pandhare, Rohit Kundaikar, Yakub Kojar, Shreyansh Tiwari
items.content: Modern healthcare generates increasingly complex medical reports that challenge clinical professionals in terms of time and interpretive burden. Manual review processes are slow, error-prone, and difficult to scale. This paper presents MeddeX, a Medical Report Analyzer that combines a QLoRA fine-tuned LLaMA-3 (8B) model with Retrieval-Augmented Gen eration (RAG) and a multimodal Gemini Vision layer to deliver accurate, concise, and evidence-backed summaries of medical documents. The system handles text-native PDFs, scanned image based PDFs, and direct radiological images through an intelligent hybrid extraction pipeline that includes a novel garbage-text detection mechanism for corrupted and UTF-16-encoded doc uments. Beyond single-report Q&A, MeddeX introduces report scoped retrieval for precise contextual grounding, an automated longitudinal report comparison engine, and a self-healing backfill pipeline that lazily processes legacy documents on demand. A FastAPI backend, Supabase vector store, and Next.js fron tend complete the end-to-end architecture. Evaluation against the base LLaMA3-Med42-8B model demonstrates consistent improvements across ROUGE-1 (+9.2%), ROUGE-2 (+10.0%), ROUGE-L (+11.8%), BLEU (+71.4%), and BERTScore (+0.8%), validating the benefit of domain-specific fine-tuning. MeddeX represents a practical and robust step toward AI-assisted clinical decision support.

items.title: Context Injection and Long-Horizon Reliability: Separating Duplicate Recognition, Local Processing, and Counter Tracking
items.author: Thomas Serval
items.content: Long-horizon failures of language models are usually measured as end-task success or as a horizon length. We instead score, step by step, three components of a 400-step ledger task in which every step is easy in isolation and the model's own answers are re-injected into its context: recognising a record already seen 5 to 300 steps earlier, processing the current record locally, and writing a counter incremented at every step. On Qwen3-8B (non-thinking, 20 seeds, replicated on a second machine and backend), with every step scored component by component, two results hold. First, duplicate-recognition errors rise late in the episode -- from 0.0019 to 0.011 per step at risk across step 200 -- while the counter makes no error in 8,000 steps and local processing is descriptively stable; the rise combines long-distance recall errors and rising false alarms. Second, a block of irrelevant content inserted before each step makes the counter fail in 20 of 20 seeds on each machine, against none without it, while its effect on local processing is much smaller and not distinguishable from none. Three pre-registered follow-ups probe the counter. Its value depends on the value present in the response history: a corrupted value persists without correction in every seed, and an exact external reminder, repeated before each message, re-aligns it within one to two steps. Under the irrelevant block, no counter error was observed when an exact compact reminder of the state, supplied externally by an oracle, preceded each message (0 of 20 seeds with an error, against 15 without it), and this reminder outperformed a length-matched neutral text; whether a single reminder suffices was not conclusive, and the absence of damage to the other components was not established. An aggregate or exclusive error classification can hide the difference we report.

items.title: Jev-as-a-Judge for RAG Claim Verification: Confidence-Gated Cascading Between a Non-Generative Verifier and a Frontier LLM
items.author: Alden Do Rosario, Kirollos Atef
items.content: Retrieval-augmented generation asks one question at volume: does this evidence support this claim? The answer is one bit, yet most pipelines obtain it from a text generator and pay generation prices for the prose wrapped around it. We compare a non-generative decision model, which returns a typed value from a declared enumeration together with a native probability and no text, against a frontier LLM configured as an engineer would deploy it for binary classification. Both answer the same 495 human-labelled claims from LLM-AggreFact, so every comparison is within-item. We report three things. First, the two systems are statistically indistinguishable on the metric this task is conventionally scored by, a paired difference of -0.56 points, Jev minus Astra, at a 187-fold cost difference. Second, that tie carries almost no information about deployment: the systems disagree on 15.2% of claims, and the cheaper one admits 23.2% of the claims annotators marked unsupported against the frontier model's 14.1%. A component whose job is to catch unsupported claims should be judged on that rate, and the conventional headline hides it. Third, because the errors differ they compose: routing the claims the cheap model is confident about and escalating the rest reaches 74.10 at USD 2.92 per thousand claims against 73.83 at USD 8.93, with the threshold chosen out of fold. But a matched random-escalation control at in-sample thresholds, spending the same budget by coin flip, does as well, so what buys the saving is the escalation share and not the probability that picks what to escalate. Measured against the cheap model it is built from, the cascade costs 61-fold more for 0.83 points, 95% CI [-3.36, 4.86], and it is the more permissive guard of the two. Equal accuracy conceals unequal errors. All predictions, prompts, pricing and code are released.

items.title: Exploring the Design Space of Permutation Diffusion LLMs
items.author: Zhe Xu, Mingfu Liang, Kavosh Asadi, Jean-Pascal Billaud, Tianyi Chen, Yanhui Guo, Christina Huang, Baekjin Kim, Jimmy Kim, Yufei Li, Daqi Sun, Jiachen Sun, Dian Yu, Zaiwei Zhang, Kaushik Rangadurai, Frank Shyu, Sandeep Pandey, Xi Liu, Luke Simon
items.content: Permutation generation with language models requires both text-conditioned ranking and a global one-to-one assignment between candidates and output positions. We study this problem through three diffusion-LLM parameterizations: hard-assignment prediction over shuffled candidate-index sequences, soft-assignment prediction over doubly stochastic matrices, and direct ordering-score prediction followed by sorting. The three families place permutation constraints at different stages of prediction and decoding and therefore support different training objectives and sampling procedures. We evaluate these designs on recommendation reranking across three Amazon domains with candidate sets of size 10 and 20. At one function evaluation, the hard- and soft-assignment variants achieve Recall@1 comparable to a constrained masked-diffusion baseline, whereas direct ordering-score prediction guarantees valid permutations without Hungarian assignment or Sinkhorn normalization. Additional function evaluations do not consistently improve ranking quality, and their effect depends strongly on the state representation and training objective. These results show that corruption, prediction parameterization, objective, and decoder should be designed jointly for permutation diffusion with language-model denoisers.

items.title: FlowBudget: Training-Free Sampling-Budget Estimation for Flow Matching Models
items.author: Zahra Dehghani, Pablo Piantanida, Mohammadhadi Shateri
items.content: Sampling from continuous flow-based generators such as flow matching models requires numerical ODE or SDE integration, making inference cost depend on the number of function evaluations (NFEs). In practice, the sampling budget is inherited from prior work or selected through expensive FID-versus-NFE sweeps, using FID to assess image-generation quality, requiring sample generation and evaluation at multiple budgets. This makes sampling-budget selection dependent on repeated empirical evaluation. We therefore ask a complementary question to solver design and timestep allocation: for a fixed pretrained model and solver, what numerical resolution is sufficient? We introduce FLOWBUDGET, a training-free estimator of solver-relative sampling complexity. Using simulation-free interpolation probes of the learned dynamics, FLOWBUDGET normalizes the leading one-step discretization error by the motion, estimates its coefficient from interpolation probes, and maps a numerical tolerance to a step budget using the solver order. We derive estimators for numerical solvers in flow~matching sampling, namely Euler and Heun for ODE sampling and additive-noise Euler--Maruyama for SDE sampling, and connect the ODE coefficients to terminal integration error. Experiments on SiT, FlowDCN and Rectified Flow models, spanning flow-model architectures and formulations, test whether FLOWBUDGET can estimate the NFE budget without generating samples at multiple budgets or performing an FID-versus-NFE sweep. The code is available at https://github.com/Yasaman-dt/FlowBudget

items.title: Expanding Attention: A Taylor-Series Route to Linear-Time Transformers with a Fixed Number of Recurrent States
items.author: Zicong Huang
items.content: We expand the exponential kernel of attention into a truncated Taylor series of $n$ terms and factorize each term into a tensor-power inner product, which collapses the causal history into exactly $n$ recurrent states, each updated by one rank-one outer product per token and independent of context length $N$. The recursion is lossless with respect to the truncated kernel ($2.2 \times 10^{-16}$ in float64), and the states are additive across chunks ($5.7 \times 10^{-14}$), so prefill admits a parallel scan. Measured exponents are $t \propto N^{2.28}$ for softmax against $N^{0.91}$ for states, with a crossover at $N \approx 728$ and $20.8\times$ at $N = 8192$; per-token decoding latency is constant at $7.3\,\mu$s against $N^{1.04}$ for softmax, giving $76.0\times$ at $N = 65536$. Accuracy improves exponentially in $n$ while cost grows combinatorially, since the $m$-th state is $\binom{d+m-1}{m}$ wide---a bound confirmed by SVD---so the optimum is second order, $n = 3$, at $6.5 \times 10^{-4}$ error and $9{,}945$ elements per head. Query and key normalization is a prerequisite: without it the argument exceeds the convergence radius and adding terms stops helping.

items.title: Feature Elicitation for SAE Steering of Deceptive Behaviour in Small LLMs
items.author: J Koorndijk
items.content: Research on deceptive alignment is becoming increasingly urgent as frontier-model capabilities advance and their risk of causing catastrophic harm increases. Alignment faking is a form of deceptive alignment, with the compliance gap serving as a key behavioural indicator. This behaviour remains understudied in small LLMs and prior mechanistic interventions have not been shown to mitigate the compliance gap. We test whether steering SAE (sparse autoencoders) features associated with deontological ethics can mitigate this behaviour. We use a novel bag-of-words feature elicitation pipeline for SAE steering to identify what we construe as concept-level steering directions. Our approach reduced the compliance gap to non-significance in Gemma-3-27B-IT, whereas the tested configurations were not effective in LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct. Analysis of scratchpad traces also revealed deceptive model behaviour which we term deceptive defanging: deliberately degrading the aligned functionality of a response (in this case harmfulness) while preserving the appearance of alignment (in this case helpful compliance with the harmful request), sometimes conditioned on tier, training, or RLHF consequences. These findings provide, to our knowledge, the first evidence that a mechanistic activation-level intervention can mitigate the compliance gap in an alignment faking setup. They also identify a form of deceptive behaviour that may broaden our understanding of the different forms of deceptive behaviour in LLMs.

items.title: Same Answer, New Box: How Much of RLVR's Out-of-Domain Gain Is Answer Format?
items.author: Zongye Lyu
items.content: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is credited with gains beyond the domain its rewards check, such as higher MMLU accuracy after training on mathematics. Such accuracies are usually read out of the model's text by an answer extractor. A model that learns to write its answer where the extractor looks can therefore score higher without answering better. We measure how much of the gain reported by extractors copied from public code arises this way. We generate outputs from a base model and its RL model and score them twice: with those extractors, and with one extractor of our own that reads a stated answer whether it is in the answer box \boxed{} or in the text. On four released 7B SimpleRL base-RL pairs, 82% of the out-of-domain multiple-choice gain that these extractors report disappears under ours: it is a gain in answer format, not in answers. The base models already state most of their answers in text, and RL moves them into the box, where these extractors look first. Independent LLM readers, in place of our extractor, put the figure at 77%. With a prompt that itself asks for the box, our extractor puts it at 79%. On a 32B pair trained with another recipe, almost none of the reported gain is format gain: its base model boxes its answers when asked, and its RL model rarely does when not. A reported gain is partly a property of the extractor that read it, and re-scoring stored outputs with a second extractor shows how much, without re-running RL.

items.title: KNOU-Flood: Advancing global streamflow forecasting with lead-aware probabilistic machine learning
items.author: Minjong Cheon
items.content: Global streamflow forecasting supports flood preparedness, yet data-driven models trained on reanalysis lose skill when driven by operational forecasts, increasingly so with lead time. AIFL addresses this shift with a two-stage transfer-learning recipe and a deterministic LSTM, but it feeds one forecast lead time into the whole input window and gives no uncertainty. We ask how far this open recipe can be extended without changing its recurrent core. KNOU-Flood keeps a single-layer LSTM and the two-stage training and changes the information around it: a longer input window (424 days), lead-aware forecast inputs, GraphCast as a second forecast source next to ECMWF HRES, and a latent-noise ensemble trained with the fair CRPS. We compare against a re-implementation of the AIFL recipe (its code is not public) under identical data, stations, splits and metrics. Our contributions are threefold. First, over three seeds and 2,099 test basins (2021-2023), KNOU-Flood reaches a median KGE' of 0.65 at LT1 and 0.48 at LT10 against 0.62 and 0.34, with significant gains at all ten lead times under two scoring protocols, also against a 1024-unit baseline and on held-out basins (one seed each). Second, identical weights give an LT10 KGE' of 0.18 or 0.34 depending on how forecasts are fed, so much of the lead-time decay reported for AIFL is an input-protocol effect; the probabilistic head contributes most to the gain, followed by the raw GraphCast channels, the longer window and mixed fine-tuning. Third, the ensembles reach lower CRPS than probabilistic versions of the baseline, are nearly calibrated with inference-time dropout, and detect 1.5- and 2-year floods better than all baselines; the benefit for rarer floods depends on the seed, and an exploratory tail-weighted variant improves 10-year and larger events. KNOU-Flood is a controlled extension of an open recipe, not a new architecture.

items.title: AbridgeKV: Compressing Long Reasoning into the KV Cache of Learned Pause Tokens
items.author: Jack Cai, Lijie Yang, Vasilis Kontonis, Dimitris Papailiopoulos, Shivam Garg
items.content: Long chain-of-thought decoding is memory-bound: the KV cache of the generated tokens grows linearly with the test-time compute being spent. Evicting cache entries does not fix this, because a model never trained on a cache with entries removed generates longer, often up to the length limit. We instead train the model to compress its own output. AbridgeKV compresses each completed block of generated text into the KV entries of a few learned pause tokens. These are extra input tokens with trained embeddings that produce no output. Once the pause tokens have encoded the block, AbridgeKV frees the block's original cache; subsequent tokens attend to the pause tokens' KV entries in its place. Three novel choices make this work: the pause tokens' KV entries take positions inside the block they replace, the cache budget is allocated across layers according to the measured value of each layer's entries, and compression operates on relatively large blocks. On 446 competition problems from AIME, HMMT, AMC, BRUMO, CMIMC and SMT with 32K-token generations, keeping a quarter of the generated cache matches an identically trained full-KV model in accuracy and output length; the strongest published evictor at a matched budget writes far longer, and the closest trained compressor, retrained on the same data, loses 10 points. Served in vLLM, the cache is 3.5x smaller per sequence and a saturated H100 finishes a problem 3.2x faster than with full KV.

items.title: CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.author: Jie Yu, Yuxi Sun, Zhaoxu Li, Chunxiao Liu, Xudong Jiang
items.content: Recent latent reasoning methods move beyond discrete Chain-of-Thought (CoT) by replacing sampled tokens with continuous soft embeddings or hidden states, enabling richer intermediate representations and preserving alternative reasoning paths. However, the need for latent reasoning varies across decoding steps: confident predictions favor discrete commitment, whereas ambiguous steps benefit from preserving multiple plausible alternatives. Existing approaches typically handle this variation through either global soft activation or hard switching based on uncertainty thresholds, treating latent intervention as an all-or-nothing decision rather than continuously adapting its strength. To address this limitation, we propose Competitive Token Selection (CoTS), a training-free framework that reframes latent intervention from binary mode selection into continuous allocation at the token level. CoTS uses the probability competition between the two most likely candidates to dynamically balance discrete commitment and soft exploration at each reasoning step. The second candidate represents the strongest alternative to the model's preferred continuation, so the separation between the two directly reflects the stability of the current discrete choice. When one candidate clearly dominates, CoTS keeps the representation close to the sampled discrete token to preserve a stable reasoning trajectory; as the competition strengthens, it increases the contribution of the soft representation to retain plausible alternatives. This competition-based allocation requires neither manually tuned switching thresholds nor mixing coefficients, and introduces no additional forward passes. Experiments across six reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that CoTS consistently outperforms standard CoT and state-of-the-art training-free latent reasoning methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/OkinoYu/CoTSReasoning.

items.title: Does Personalization Break Trust? Open-Set Rejection Calibration Under Few-Shot On-Device Intent Adaptation
items.author: Vaibhav Prajapati, Pushp Garg
items.content: Always-on virtual assistants increasingly personalize on-device to new user-specific commands via few-shot fine-tuning (e.g., LoRA), but this adaptation is evaluated almost exclusively on whether it learns the new commands, not on whether the assistant can still recognize an input that matches none of its intents - the out-of-scope (OOS) rejection problem. We show that naive few-shot LoRA personalization degrades OOS-rejection AUROC (area under the ROC curve) on every one of five public intent-classification benchmarks (mean drop $0.055$--$0.258$, five seeds each), while in-scope accuracy is preserved. A scorer-invariant check shows part of this drop is an artifact of the standard confidence scorer's own miscalibration under adaptation, though a smaller, genuine effect remains under any scorer; we trace it to a measurable shrinkage of the embedding margin around known-intent regions (pooled Spearman rho=0.61$). A deployment-cheap fix is scoring rejection by Mahalanobis distance instead of softmax confidence without extra training/retraining recovers most of the lost quality on 3 of 5 datasets at no accuracy cost, beats two further OOD scoring baselines, and generalizes across shot count, LoRA rank, and a second base encoder. We report honestly where the fix falls short and release all code for reproducibility.

items.title: The World Won't Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock
items.author: Ningxin Pan, Hanyu Li, Yeqing Shen, Ning Ding, Yehui Tang, Wentao Zhang
items.content: Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late. We introduce RealtimeBench, with 180 tasks across six game types, to evaluate agents while games continue running during inference. Paired evaluations show that GPT-6.1-sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when they keep running. We propose Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (TORSI): a slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts, then writes reusable instructions for a fast student. The student acts without teacher calls during gameplay, and validation scores determine which updates are adopted. Two rounds raise Jev's average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0--100 progress scale, improving all six game types. The instructions also improve average scores for three other models without retuning. These findings point toward real-time intelligence: enabling powerful LLM agents to remain effective in a continuously changing world by organizing deliberation, learning, and action across timescales.

items.title: Evaluating Model Capabilities After Benchmark Saturation
items.author: Morio Hamada, Jehyeok Yeon, Matteo Migliarini, Justin Olive, Magda Dubois
items.content: Rapid advances in AI capabilities are causing benchmarks to saturate. Once several models approach perfect scores, a benchmark loses its power to differentiate between them, and with it its utility for informing AI safety cases and frontier policies. Yet benchmark items produce far more information than the scores we typically extract from them: a full transcript of how each model solved the task. We investigate whether these transcripts can be used to assess model capabilities even after benchmark scores have saturated. We simulate saturation retrospectively using historical benchmark and model releases, and test whether protocols that access only correctly solved transcripts from saturated benchmarks can predict capabilities measured on held-out, unsaturated items. We evaluate representative contemporary approaches for extracting information from model transcripts: pairwise judging, single-transcript absolute scoring, and predictions from deterministic transcript features or embeddings. We find that saturated transcripts retain capability information beyond benchmark accuracy. Amongst our evaluated protocols, pairwise judging performs best, reducing prediction error by 5.3 times compared to a baseline using only saturated benchmark scores. This capability-relevant information is distributed across transcript sections, but concentrated in specific channels of information such as reasoning and tool-calls. However, the predictive power of protocols does not always generalise across distribution shifts -- for example by underestimating the capabilities of the first reasoning models introduced in early 2025. Saturated benchmarks thus retain capability-predicting signal in their task transcripts, but extending the lifetime of existing benchmarks requires methods designed to extract these signals robustly.

items.title: Value-Informed Schedule Trimming for Accelerated Sequential Monte Carlo Guidance in Discrete Diffusion
items.author: Jaehyeon Kim, Ziseok Lee, Siyoung Choi, Kyungsu Kim
items.content: Reward-guided discrete diffusion enables test-time alignment with downstream objectives, but applying Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) guidance at every denoising step is computationally expensive. Active guidance steps require additional reward evaluations and, for gradient-based proposals, value-gradient computations. Sparse guidance reduces this cost by guiding only a subset of timesteps, but commonly used schedules are fixed heuristics whose effectiveness can vary substantially across tasks. We propose VISTA, a training-free method that automatically selects guided timesteps under a fixed budget. VISTA formulates sparse guidance as approximation of the ideal full-guidance probability path and derives an estimable upper bound on \(\ell_1\) path deviation. Using value statistics collected from a small number of full-guidance warmup generations, VISTA optimizes the resulting empirical surrogate exactly via dynamic programming. The warmup generations can be retained as model outputs, and after schedule selection VISTA has the same per-generation guidance complexity as other sparse schedules with the same budget. Across text, biological sequence, and image generation tasks, VISTA discovers task-dependent schedules and outperforms hand-designed sparse schedules in most tested settings, while approaching or exceeding full-guidance performance on several task metrics. In toxic-text generation, for example, VISTA attains a 0.99 unique-toxic ratio compared with 1.00 for full guidance while reducing post-selection per-generation latency from 204.23 s to 38.16 s, a 5.35$\times$ speedup.

items.title: AlphaDiana: A Measurement System for Agents in Verifiable Reasoning Tasks
items.author: Zhanke Zhou, Zongze Li, Weikai Huang, Xuan Li, Chentao Cao, Xiao Feng, Xiangyu Lu, Jinbo Hu, Yi Xie, Nico Pelleriti, Shiyang Liu, Menghan Lu, Max Zimmer, Brando Miranda, Jiangchao Yao, Bo Liu, Sanmi Koyejo, Sebastian Pokutta, Bo Han
items.content: Agents pair reasoning models with harnesses that organize model calls, execute tools, load skill instructions, and retain history in memory. Understanding agent performance requires linking execution conditions to outcomes, behavior, and resource use. We introduce AlphaDiana, a measurement system with modular interfaces for datasets, agents, environments, and scorers. It preserves harness-native control loops while controlling file reuse and memory retention separately. AlphaDiana supports macro analyses of complete agents and micro interventions on agent components such as tools, skills, and memory under matched conditions. We study three open-source models and three open-source harnesses on five answer-based benchmarks, with two models also tested on two interactive benchmarks. We find that harnesses do not consistently improve the accuracy of reasoning: gains on questions unsolved by the model alone can be outweighed by losses on questions it answers correctly without tools. This inconsistency extends to component interventions: neither skill guidance nor retained history reliably improves accuracy. Behavior and output-token use must be assessed with correctness: low token entropy can accompany wrong answers, and less output per execution can mean more output tokens per correct answer when accuracy falls. AlphaDiana links answer correctness and execution status to traces and resource records for comparing agents and diagnosing failures under shared task and resource policies.

items.title: When Correctness Feedback Erases Evidence: Phase-Separated Completeness Auditing in Verus
