items.author: Adarsh Agrawal (Independent Researcher)
items.content: Correctness feedback suppresses the very evidence that specification-completeness auditing is designed to uncover: programs that satisfy a written contract but violate intended behavior. We demonstrate this objective reversal on 12 Verus/Rust tasks across four model families under matched call budgets. Independent no-feedback discovery more than doubles certified-witness yield relative to IntentShield's corrective-feedback loop (59.0% versus 27.1%). A format-matched iterative control places the larger share of this gap in feedback content, not independent restarts. The advantage holds in every model family and survives parser repair. A separate phase-separated execution matches the aggregate yield without reusing responses; most certified witnesses also fail held-out cases. Preserving these witnesses delivers stronger specification repair: Phase-Revised contracts achieve 81.3% implementation success, versus 62.5% for IS-Revised, with Direct-Revised close behind. Both no-feedback witness sources substantially outperform weakened contracts. The effect does not reproduce in the available Dafny and Lean evaluations, establishing an empirical boundary around the studied Verus/Rust workflow. Completeness auditing and correctness repair have opposing immediate objectives. Preserve and certify the admitted failure before repairing it.

items.title: Spectral Indistinguishability and Learning-Curve Identifiability in Quadratic Networks
items.author: Dekun Yang
items.content: We study what spectral summaries and scalar learning curves reveal about centered quadratic networks. We construct analytic positive input densities with exactly Gaussian one- and two-coordinate marginals. Their complete fourth-moment operators are intertwined by an orthogonal map fixing the entire diagonal teacher algebra, so the corresponding anchored spectral measures agree. For selected common teachers with a nonzero cycle invariant, their factorized loss curves differ because the map does not preserve matrix multiplication. Cycle length $r$, which can be arbitrarily large, gives $O(\varepsilon^r)$ contrast uniformly in training time for each fixed construction. For a supplied pair, noisy scalar loss queries require order $\varepsilon^{-2r}$ observations, while bounded initialization interventions with scalar gradient readouts require order $\varepsilon^{-2}$. A shared-input score, equal to a paired-gradient difference, attains the optimal input-sample exponent without knowing the teacher. An explicit family of diverging auxiliary teacher scales instead admits a nonzero finite limiting contrast at coupling $1/\log L$. Conversely, for Gaussian inputs and a rationally independent teacher spectrum, one exact scalar loss curve identifies the initial predictor up to sign conjugation. Within this rationally independent class, with nonzero diagonal inverse-state error in every coordinate and calibrated time and loss scales, it also identifies the unknown teacher spectrum and active dimension, modulo simultaneous rotations. For fixed dimension and distinct unordered teacher sums, dimension-minimal exact observations give generic joint local recovery. Finite exact global bounds hold for a known teacher and, on the active class, under a blind dimension cap. Exact certificates and full-weight replay verify the construction; numerical inverse checks reveal severe ill-conditioning.

items.title: Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields: Evidence-Grounded Selective Safety for Vision-Language Models
items.author: Tianshi Wang, Jingsong Wang, Fengling Li, Jingjing Li, Xin Li, Lei Zhu
items.content: Representation-based safety defenses for vision-language models (VLMs) often learn to separate harmful from benign inputs, but separation alone does not establish what a risk score means or when it should be trusted. We introduce Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields (CNRF), an evidence-grounded framework for selective VLM safety. CNRF constructs context-matched benign-harmful counterfactual pairs, uses their representation differences as capability-related risk directions, and estimates neighborhood support separately from risk. This separation prevents unfamiliarity from being conflated with harmfulness and enables selective intervention rather than blanket rejection. A victim-adaptive interface accommodates different safety observations across VLM architectures and routes selected requests for same-victim response review, which either releases acceptable candidates or produces constrained alternatives with reduced harmful capability. Across three VLMs and five multimodal jailbreak families, CNRF achieves 86.06-89.30% macro defense success rate while retaining substantial benign-task utility. Controlled experiments further show that query-matched references and preserved context-direction correspondence materially improve risk ranking in the low-false-positive regime. CNRF thus reframes representation-based VLM safety from learning harmfulness boundaries to constructing applicable evidence for selective risk decisions.

items.title: Diminishing Returns of Data in Sparse Autoencoders: Functional Behavior does not Guarantee Feature Reproducibility
items.author: Sambit Ghosh, Madelyn Mathai, R. Venkatesh Babu, Chirag Agarwal
items.content: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are typically trained on hundreds of millions to billions of activation tokens, yet little work has tested whether this scale is necessary. We study how much activation data SAEs need by training four SAE architectures on three language models with budgets ranging from 5M tokens to a 500M-token reference. We measure two notions of convergence: functional behavior on standard evaluations and one-to-one reproducibility of learned features. Functional data requirements are strongly metric-dependent: reconstruction often approaches the full-data reference at substantially smaller budgets, whereas feature reproducibility continues to improve with data. For Gemma-2-2B BatchTopK, the fraction of strictly matched features rises from 2\% at 5M tokens to 29\% at 50M. Data selection also matters: random sampling better preserves the original activation distribution and generally favors reconstruction, whereas diversity-based sampling frequently improves AutoInterp. A theoretical analysis separates statistical consistency of subsampled training from the stronger identifiability and optimization conditions required for one-to-one feature recovery. Our results show that SAE training can often be made far more data-efficient when budgets are matched to the goal, and feature-level claims are backed by explicit reproducibility checks, paving the way toward cheaper and more reliable SAE research.

items.title: IneqAgent: Agentic Inequality Proving in Lean with Symbolic Computation
items.author: Gaolei He, Jinhui Li, Ruobing Zuo, Xia Zeng, Zhengfeng Yang
items.content: Formal inequality proving requires mathematical reasoning and exact computation, often connected through intermediate lemmas and goal reformulations. We introduce IneqAgent, an agentic framework combining LLM reasoning with symbolic computation for inequality proving in Lean4. Lemma-level Monte Carlo Tree Search coordinates lemma construction, goal reformulation, and symbolic backend selection. Complementary sum-of-squares, Bernstein, and successive difference-substitution backends produce exact certificates for local Lean proof generation. The agent integrates these proofs with LLM-generated steps and uses Lean feedback to construct complete proofs checked against the original theorem statements. On four benchmarks, IneqAgent with DeepSeek-V4-Flash solves 175 of 186 problems (94.09%), achieving the highest overall success rate among the evaluated methods. Across four backbones, it achieves higher success rates at low LLM inference cost thresholds than Direct Agent using the same backbone, with lower mean inference costs over each method's successful runs. We also obtain Lean-verified strengthenings of Dittert's conjecture in dimensions four and five, and certify the Holens--Djokovic $(4,4)$ inequality, implying Merris's conjecture in dimension four.

items.title: Harnessing MPI mutations for AI error detection
items.author: Asia Auville (STORM, TADAAM), Tim Jammer (TU Darmstadt), Eric Petit (LI-PaRAD), Pablo de Oliveira Castro (LI-PaRAD, UVSQ), Emmanuelle Saillard (STORM), Mihail Popov (TADAAM)
items.content: MPI errors are challenging to identify despite the significant number of expert verification tools. Dynamic tools (i.e., requiring profiling) are computationally expensive and accurate in error detection, whereas static analysis (i.e., operating at source code or compilation) is computationally cheap but less accurate. Interestingly, the recent success of AI and LLMs offers an alternative to increase static analysis accuracy while preserving its low overhead. Yet current methods remain difficult to benchmark, too general, and poorly adapted to the specific challenges of high-performance computing. In this paper, we investigate how AI-powered tools can efficiently and accurately detect errors in real-world MPI applications. We propose a novel MPI Mutated Dataset (MMD), constructed from MPI programs extracted from thousands of open-source GitHub projects. After sorting and filtering these files, we inject errors that realistically emulate developers' mistakes using synthetic code mutations. We leverage the dataset to train different AI models and assess their generalization capabilities against standard verification tools. We train compact multilayer perceptrons (MLP) with AST-T5 embeddings (i.e., transformer only encoder network) to detect diverse MPI errors (from the MPI-BugBench (MBB) classification) including CallOrdering or InvalidParameter, achieving detection accuracies up to 92.0%. In some cases, our method outperforms the expert prompted Qwen-3 Coder LLM and provides competitive results compared to established dynamic verification tools. We further evaluate Claude Sonnet 4.5 across different prompting strategies, showing that engineered prompts improve InvalidParam detection accuracy from 84.8% to 93.6%, surpassing the dynamic tool ITAC (87.0%). The full agentic pipeline achieves 73.9% overall multi-class accuracy and 87.6% bug detection recall on MBB. This paves the way for large-scale verification efforts that can use our dataset as a foundation to thoroughly investigate each MPI error in real world applications.

items.title: Developer Experiences with Cursor AI-native IDE
items.author: Haoran Xue, Gias Uddin, Song Wang
items.content: AI-powered integrated development environments (IDEs) are increasingly positioned as practical tools for software development, integrating AI assistance into everyday activities such as editing, refactoring, and debugging. However, how developers evaluate AI IDEs as working environments, what frictions shape their adoption, and which aspects of the experience matter most in everyday use remain underexplored. Prior evidence on adoption and use is mainly controlled tasks, small interview samples, and short observation windows, which offer limited visibility into longitudinal, community-driven experience and the workflow drift that emerges in everyday practice. To bridge this gap, we conduct a large-scale longitudinal study of Cursor, a prominent AI-native IDE, through its official public forum, where users report bugs, request features, and discuss everyday use. Our analysis covers 14,714 forum posts collected over more than two years. We find that discussion is dominated by workflow-critical mechanisms (71%) such as context indexing, model routing, and agent workflows, which are also the main sources of both perceived value and frustration. Negative experiences center on usability, pricing, and dependability, including installation and setup, usage limits and consumption, crashes, and latency. Over time, the focus of friction shifts from early access and setup barriers toward pricing, robustness, and sustained workflow reliability.

items.title: Forensic Analysis of the HackRF One with PortaPack Mayhem Firmware
items.author: D\"uzg\"un K\"u\c{c}\"uk
items.content: Software-defined radios (SDRs) have become an inexpensive, portable platform for replay attacks, location spoofing and jamming. The HackRF One can operate stand-alone when fitted with a PortaPack interface board running the open-source Mayhem firmware. No peer-reviewed study has addressed the forensic analysis of this device family. This work establishes, at source-code level, where forensically relevant data reside on the microSD card of a device running Mayhem v2.0.1, in which format, when they are written and how they should be interpreted. The methodology is applied to an SD card image that the author acquired from their own device after four months of real use, and every inference is drawn from the image alone. The workflow covers timestamp rules that depend on the real-time clock (RTC) battery state, traces of on-device trimming and text editing, cluster-level recovery of deleted in-phase/quadrature (IQ) captures, and decoding of recorded signals cross-checked with an independent decoder. In the example image, the final part of a deleted IQ capture and a trimmed-away capture segment are recovered, and six captures are attributed to a single rolling-code on-off keying (OOK) transmitter sharing one 32-bit identifier. The study provides practitioners with an artifact catalogue, interpretation rules and acquisition recommendations.

items.title: Unmasking the Secret Code: Using Canaries to Show How Masked Context Controls Memorization in SFT
items.author: Avi Schwarzschild, Om Thakkar, Sahra Ghalebikesabi, Congzheng Song, Vinnie Monaco
items.content: Canaries, or synthetic training records containing known secrets, are widely used to assess whether language models reveal information from their training data. But how much do these measurements depend on the canaries themselves? We study this question through controlled fine-tuning experiments with language and vision-language models, spanning synthetic tasks and tasks where training improves useful performance. Whether a secret is provided in the training input strongly changes what the model learns; for example, models can reproduce a secret in the input yet fail to recall it when it is removed, even after extensive repetition during training. When training instead requires predicting the secret from the surrounding context, later recall can become reliable. Repetition alone is therefore insufficient to characterize memorization. We also find that changing when a canary appears, or which other canaries accompany it, can substantially change measured memorization without increasing that canary's repetition count. These results show that canary measurements depend on how secrets are presented during training and tested afterward. Audits should test whether their conclusions hold across these choices before extending them to other training records.

items.title: Empirical Evaluation of Machine Learning for Cloud Cryptojacking Detection: Effects of Preprocessing and Evaluation Protocols
items.author: Amitabh Chakravorty, Nelly Elsayed
items.content: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied to cloud cryptojacking detection. Classical machine learning models remain among the most widely used approaches for cloud cryptojacking detection. This paper presents an empirical evaluation of six widely used classical machine learning models for AI-based cloud cryptojacking detection under different preprocessing and evaluation settings. Because no public cloud-native cryptojacking dataset is currently available, experiments were conducted using two publicly available proxy datasets, DS2OS and NSL-KDD. The evaluated models include Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, Decision Tree, and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN). Experimental results show that preprocessing choices and evaluation protocols have a measurable impact on model performance. On DS2OS, removing identifier-related features reduced the accuracy of most models to approximately 96%, while KNN achieved higher accuracy with lower attack recall. On NSL-KDD, models obtained 77 to 80\% accuracy on the official test set containing unseen attack types, compared with above 99.5% under a random train-test split. Attack-class precision, recall, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) further provide complementary insights into classifier performance beyond overall accuracy. The results provide an empirical comparison of commonly used classical machine learning models under consistent experimental settings and offer insights into how preprocessing, dataset selection, and evaluation methodology influence reported performance.

items.title: Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network for Interpretable Big Data Analytics and Secure Cloud Decision-Making Systems
items.author: B. Nancharaiah, Ramakrishna Kolikipogu, J. Sulthan Alikhan, Lakshmana Phaneendra Maguluri, Elangovan Muniyandy, D. Baburao
items.content: Big data analytics supports modern intelligent systems, but model complexity and limited transparency can undermine interpretability, trust, and security in decision-making. This paper presents the Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network, a deep learning framework that integrates temporal, relational, and contextual features with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) mechanisms. The architecture combines one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) for temporal feature extraction, Transformer encoders for contextual modeling, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for inter-feature dependency analysis. An attention-based fusion mechanism integrates these representations. Class Activation Mapping (CAM) and an explanation loss are incorporated to improve interpretability and explanation consistency. The framework is designed for deployment in a federated cloud architecture, using homomorphic encryption and blockchain-based auditing to support data privacy and accountability. Experimental evaluations across healthcare, finance, and energy datasets report 98.42% accuracy, 97.9% precision, 98.1% recall, and a 98.0% F1-score, outperforming the evaluated CNN-LSTM, Transformer-only, and XGBoost baselines. Under projected gradient descent (PGD) adversarial perturbations, the model reportedly retains accuracy above 91.5%. Scalability experiments report throughput of 80,000 messages per second with latency below 200 milliseconds. These results suggest that the proposed framework has potential for interpretable and secure cloud-based decision-support systems.

items.title: CascadeLedger: Counterfactual Auditing of Information and Resource Integrity in LLM Cascades
items.author: Miaobo Hu, Shuhao Hu, Xiaobo Guo, Xin Wang, Bokun Wang, Daren Zha, Jun Xiao
items.content: We introduce CascadeLedger, a counterfactual execution-audit framework for budgeted language-model cascades. The protocol enforces call-before-read semantics, binds successful reads to service and cache identities, records availability and component-wise budget transitions, and freezes the event trace before any target or task scorer is joined. The central object is aggregate-equivalent trace validity: two executions can share a final answer, declared resource projection, and service histogram while differing in whether their routing decisions used only legitimately observable information. We complement single-trace invariants with counterfactual prefix non-interference (CPNI), which couples a visible prefix and policy randomness while changing only a declared hidden family. The counterfactual influence frontier (CIF) localizes the earliest violating prefix and a minimal hidden witness; projection-preserving adversarial mutation (PPAM) searches for invalid traces that remain acceptable to a non-counterfactual checker. Across frozen-cache, independently generated, and serving evaluations, the two-layer audit reports a clean false-positive rate of 0.0000, detects 0.9983 of serialized faults and 0.9982 of unlogged hidden-read faults, and changes 0.3403 of corrupted quality-resource conclusions after deterministic recomputation. The online recorder and offline CPNI audit have separate overhead measurements. Learned routing and semantic verification provide downstream compatibility studies under the same execution contract.

items.title: HPCAgent-Bench: A Framework for Sound Benchmarking of Code-Optimizing Agents, Harnesses, and Skills
items.author: Yakup Koray Budanaz, Lorenzo Paleari, Marcin Copik, Alexandru Calotoiu, Timo Schneider, Benjamin Chen Ming Choong, Shriram Chandran, Lars Hulsbergen, Levi Widmer, Torsten Hoefler
items.content: Coding agents are increasingly used to optimize code, but existing benchmarks fix one accelerator, programming model or harness, so they cannot isolate what each component contributes or show whether added skills and tools repay their cost. We present HPCAgent-Bench with 689 kernels in three tracks: loop-level optimization challenges, kernels extracted from HPC codes, and machine-learning models. The framework specifies each kernel once in NumPy, derives C and Fortran references, accepts submissions through a common C ABI or Python interface, and runs them on CPUs or GPUs, on one or multiple nodes. An external judge checks correctness on hidden fuzzed inputs and times each submission, closing paths agents use to exploit the testing system. We introduce two metrics for reporting results: \textit{intervention efficacy} measures an intervention, such as adding a tool, through paired runs on speedup, success rate and cost, and \textit{weighted token cost} reports input, cached-input and output tokens under explicit weights. Agents reach up to $4.2\times$ speedup over automatic parallelizers, and their optimizations transfer to another machine: $93$--$99\%$ of answers without device-specific code remain correct, and per-kernel speedups keep a rank correlation of $r_s\ge0.84$. Across 40 matched setups, interventions significantly change speedup only twice but token cost by up to $3.0\times$. Because token weighting decides whether a saving is significant, we state the weights and release every token count as a standard for cost reporting. We provide the first comprehensive, broad and hardened benchmark for the sound evaluation of agentic optimization, with transparent cost metrics.

items.title: Foundations of Hardware-Software Leakage Contracts
items.author: Jan Reineke
items.content: Microarchitectural attacks such as Spectre and Meltdown undermine security by exploiting software-visible side effects of microarchitectural optimizations like caches and speculative execution. To use modern hardware securely, programmers must take into account the security implications of these optimizations. Yet instruction set architectures (ISAs)---the conventional abstraction layer between hardware and software---are ill-suited for secure programming: by design, they abstract from microarchitectural details and therefore fail to reflect their security consequences. A new security abstraction is emerging to fill this void: hardware-software leakage contracts. To support the principled development of secure software on modern hardware such contracts characterize side-channel leakage at the ISA level. Thereby they enable programmers and compilers to generate code that is provably resistant to side-channel attacks---without having to explicitly reason about the microarchitecture. On the other hand, they provide a specification for hardware designers to ensure that microarchitectures do not introduce unintended and undocumented side channels. This paper introduces the foundations of this emerging topic, discussing recent contributions and unresolved challenges along the way.

items.title: INFUSE: A Unified Surface Benchmark for Indirect Prompt Injection in Agentic Systems
items.author: Thuy Dung Nguyen, Jingyi Guo, Rana Seda Dubauskas, Sreepriya Damuluru, Taylor T. Johnson, Kevin Leach
items.content: LLM-based agents increasingly execute long-horizon, end-to-end workflows involving shell commands, code modification, dependency installation, and interaction with remote services. This growing autonomy expands their exposure to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in external content are interpreted as legitimate task directives. Existing evaluations, however, often focus on isolated malicious strings, single-step tool calls, or narrowly scoped agent configurations. We introduce INFUSE, an end-to-end benchmark for evaluating IPI throughout the lifecycle of long-horizon agent workflows. INFUSE comprises 40 realistic tasks and a structured taxonomy of 56 attack scenarios spanning five threat categories. Attacks are injected through realistic interaction surfaces encountered during task execution, extending evaluation beyond attacks placed only in initial prompts or isolated tool interactions. We evaluate 19 LLMs from the GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, producing 41,824 adversarial trajectories (26,220 without defenses) and 720 benign reference runs. Across the benchmark, mean attack success reaches 19.6% under LLM-based evaluation and 15.4% under heuristic verification, with per-model ASR-L ranging from 3.2% to 41.9%. Existing guard models provide limited protection, while prompt-level instructional hardening reduces mean attack success from 58.2% to 14.3%, revealing substantial but model-dependent security-utility trade-offs. Our code is available at https://github.com/judydnguyen/infuse.

items.title: Privacy-Preserving Text Inference for Health-Misinformation Classification and Semantic Retrieval
items.author: Jasleen Kaur, Chlo\'e Cachet, Koray Karabina, Jean Belo Klamti, Philippe Lamontagne
items.content: Health-misinformation analysis presents a dual challenge: misleading claims can affect public well-being, while systems designed to detect them may expose sensitive user-submitted text. This motivates privacy-preserving inference for public-health applications in which user queries may contain confidential medical information and trained models and reference databases are maintained on organizational servers. We design a privacy-preserving text inference framework based on CKKS homomorphic encryption for health-misinformation classification and semantic retrieval. The classification pipeline fuses BioBERT embeddings, PCA-reduced MPNet embeddings, and SVD-reduced TF-IDF features, while the retrieval pipeline combines MPNet embeddings with ISCC-SCT semantic fingerprints through late fusion. We evaluate predictive performance and benchmark plaintext versus ciphertext-based execution. The hybrid classifier achieved an accuracy of 0.971 and a macro-F1 score of 0.950, with identical reported metrics under plaintext and ciphertext-based inference. The hybrid late-fusion similarity model achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.8691 with human sentence-pair similarity scores on STS-B. For ciphertext-based retrieval, we evaluated naive and optimized implementations. The optimized implementation uses CKKS single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) packing to compute and return multiple similarity scores together, reducing single-query latency over 7,128 indexed items from 222.028 to 5.168 seconds and communication overhead from 6.11 GB to 2.13 MB. These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of privacy-preserving text inference for health-misinformation applications and characterize its predictive utility and efficiency trade-offs.

items.title: Robotic-supported Data Loss Detection in Android Applications
items.author: Davi Freitas, Breno Miranda, Juliano Iyoda
items.content: Smartphones have become integral to modern life due to their diverse applications. However, the development of applications for these devices faces significant challenges, primarily due to two factors: (i) the diverse hardware and operating system versions that require testing across multiple configurations; and (ii) the imperative activity of testing the smartphone in a non-invasive way (similar to an end-user interaction), which is expensive, tedious and error-prone as it is usually carried out manually. In this context, robotic automation has emerged as an effective solution for addressing the diversity of smartphone systems and versions, and in performing some testing tasks non-invasively. In addition, automated robots facilitate quick, accurate, and repetitive testing, thus enabling developers to validate their applications across various configurations effectively. This results in a less invasive verification and in a significant reduction in time spent on manual testing, thus accelerating the development cycle. Our work proposes R-DLD (Robotic-supported Data Loss Detection), a robot-assisted infrastructure for data loss detection in Android applications, offeringless invasive and more realistic tests by interacting directly with smartphone sensors. The robot is constructed using cost-effective materials, facilitating its adoption in testing environments. In our empirical evaluation R-DLD successfully identified 341 data loss issues in 77 randomly selected apps from an Android store. All reported bugs received responses from the developer, with 89.55% confirming the data loss problems, while 35.82% have being subsequently fixed.

items.title: Performance Characterization of Pulsar's Software-defined Watermark Verifier
items.author: Jason Anderson, Kaz Gunning
items.content: Pulsar provides the world's most secure PNT service by incorporating a Combinatorial Watermark into its ranging service. Under conservative signal conditions, Pulsar's Combinatorial Watermark, where 21 ranging code chips are inverted among the 1023, provides 32-bit authentication security each second. In this work, we present our software-defined radio (SDR) implementation of the Pulsar watermark processor. We discuss various threat models, multiple receiver architectures, implications to the receiver, and results from using Pulsar's SDR processing watermarked signals daily from the Pulsar-0 mission. Our results demonstrate the feasible implementation of Pulsar's watermark verification process in commercial GNSS receivers. This is an important milestone in making Xona's Pulsar service available to customers later this year after deployment of our first four production satellites.

items.title: GhostLock: Learning-Assisted Blind GPS Signal Nullification Without Victim-Side Information
items.author: Khalil Ahmad, Omar Ansari, Mohsin Kamal, Asif Iqbal, Muhammad Naveed Aman
items.content: The Global Positioning System (GPS) provides critical positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services for numerous safety- and mission-critical applications, making it an attractive target for physical-layer attacks. While GPS spoofing and jamming have been extensively studied, GPS Signal Nullification (GSN)-a physical-layer attack that suppresses authentic satellite signals through destructive interference prior to acquisition-remains largely unexplored. Existing wireless signal nullification techniques target conventional communication systems and typically require victim-side information, such as channel estimates or synchronization parameters, making them impractical for GPS. Furthermore, many GPS spoofing defenses assume authentic satellite signals remain available as trusted references, an assumption invalidated by GSN. To address this gap, we present GhostLock, a learning-assisted blind GSN framework requiring only an approximate target location estimate. GhostLock integrates a Blind Adaptive Filter (BAF) with a deep learning-based synchronization module to generate and align an anti-signal using only the attacker's locally received GPS signal, eliminating the need for victim-side observations. We implement GhostLock on a real-time software-defined radio (SDR) platform using GPS-SDR-SIM and GNU Radio. Experimental results demonstrate successful suppression of GPS signal acquisition, establishing the feasibility of blind GSN and motivating new detection and mitigation techniques for this emerging GPS threat model.

items.title: Thinking in Graphs: Neo4j-Backed Exploit-Chain Reasoning for LLM Penetration-Testing Agents
items.author: Joas Antonio dos Santos Barbosa
items.content: LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can drive penetration-testing tools, but they reason about an engagement as a flat list of findings in a context window. Attackers think in graphs: isolated low-severity exposures turn catastrophic once chained through credential capture, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This gap feeds a common belief that AI agents cannot truly chain exploitation; we argue this describes the flat context window, not the model. We present ChainGraph, a pattern that externalizes exploit-chain reasoning into a Neo4j property graph wired to an off-the-shelf agent via the Model Context Protocol, no bespoke harness. Findings, attack steps, credentials, assets, and tamper-evident evidence receipts are typed nodes with pre/post-condition edges; JSON/Markdown holds documentary memory while Neo4j holds reasoning memory. We formalize five operator questions (next-step inference, entry-to-crown-jewel pathing, combined-severity promotion, evidence provenance, and chokepoint identification) as reusable Cypher and Graph Data Science queries, plus a chain-severity score distinct from per-finding local severity. On a synthetic multi-forest Active Directory engagement modeled on GOAD, in live Neo4j with GDS, three findings rated Medium in isolation become Critical once their path to the forest root is materialized, and betweenness centrality names the best chain break-points. Scoping each decision to a graph result rather than re-reading the engagement cut the reasoning payload by about 98% on a token proxy. We give a reproducible setup for Claude Code and Codex. Results are illustrative single-run measurements, not a benchmark.

items.title: From Detection to Decision: Calibration and Deferral for Prompt-Injection Detection
items.author: Qianlong Lan, Anuj Kaul, Vinothini Pandurangan, Indranil Sanyal
items.content: Prompt-injection defenses are commonly evaluated as binary detectors, although deployed LLM applications must make operational decisions about whether to allow, block, or escalate potentially malicious inputs. Recent probabilistic decision models aim to support such decisions through calibrated confidence estimates, but their reliability under distribution shift remains uncertain. We evaluate a native probabilistic decision model (Jev), two Llama Prompt Guard 2 classifiers (22M and 86M), and an LLM-based judge on 47,611 held-out examples spanning direct and indirect prompt injections, hard-benign inputs, obfuscation, and distribution shift. Using separate development and calibration splits, we assess detection performance, probability calibration, and allow-block-defer policies under a frozen evaluation protocol. The LLM judge achieves the highest overall discrimination (AUROC 0.897), followed by Jev (0.871), Prompt Guard 2 86M (0.757), and Prompt Guard 2 22M (0.714). However, Jev's native probabilities do not consistently outperform post-hoc calibrated classifier scores, and temperature scaling improves calibration without improving discrimination. At an empirical false-negative-rate target of 1%, all evaluated gate-reviewer systems require more than 91.8% escalation and incur substantial false-positive rates. These findings demonstrate that probabilistic outputs alone do not establish reliable security decisions under distribution shift. Effective LLM security systems must jointly evaluate detection, calibration, reviewer behavior, and operational decision policies.

items.title: Screwtape: Adversarial Transcript Editing for Monitor Red-Teaming
items.author: Gosha Kozhevnikov, Tyler Tracy
items.content: We present Screwtape, a pipeline that converts real agent transcripts into attacks that evade action-only monitors. An LLM attacker edits a transcript so that the agent causes a specified harm, such as leaking an API key or spawning an unmonitored agent. The edited actions are never executed, so we use an LLM verifier to reject attacks that are inconsistent with the original transcript or below a severity bar. The attacker revises the edit until the monitor no longer flags it. We applied Screwtape to 94 Claude Code and Codex transcripts from Redwood Research staff, optimizing against our own monitors. Across 252 runs, it produced 35 attacks that passed the verifier and evaded these monitors. Six of them, confirmed valid by human review, also evaded a held-out monitor provided by a frontier developer. We therefore demonstrate that a red-teamer without access to a developer's infrastructure can find confirmed failures of the developer's monitor. We expect to find more attacks when the pipeline runs inside the developer's infrastructure, with frontier attacker models that lack refusal safeguards and direct optimization against the production monitor. Developers can use these attacks to fix monitor blind spots, and evaluators can use them as counterexamples to safety claims about the monitor.

items.title: Does Client Diversity Protect the Lightning Network? Evidence from the 2026 Core Lightning Shutdown
items.author: Saurabh Kumar
items.content: Client diversity is often cited as the Lightning Network's defence against a bug in any one implementation, yet LND runs 84% of public nodes and holds 84% of public channel capacity, a share that has barely moved since 2023. We test what diversity buys with a natural experiment. On 26 August 2026, amid security fixes in every implementation, Core Lightning (CLN) maintainers told operators who could not upgrade to disconnect their nodes. Using 805 daily gossip snapshots, 132,360 on-chain channel closes and a client classifier validated against self-identifying aliases and against the wallet that builds each node's funding transactions, we find that 22% of CLN nodes went dark overnight, ten times the usual rate, mostly Tor-reachable ones; a third were still dark five weeks later. The rest of the network barely noticed. Reachability among all node pairs fell by 7.8 percentage points, a loss exceeded in 4 of 94 ordinary two-day windows and half that of a Tor denial-of-service wave in July, while among CLN pairs it fell by 24.5 points, more than in any ordinary window. Calibrated failure scenarios explain the containment: the blast radius depends on whether a failure reaches the hubs, not on how many nodes run the failing software. Losing ACINQ's Eclair node alone costs the surviving network four times the reachability lost with all 619 routable CLN nodes, and minority clients' reliance on LND for connectivity is what their size implies; CLN nodes in fact peer with each other more than chance. Diversity statistics that count nodes mislead; the quantity to track is which software the hubs run.

items.title: PAGE404: Breaking GPU Isolation Through Hardware-assisted Page Migration
items.author: Ravan Nazaraliyev, Yicheng Zhang, Nael Abu-Ghazaleh
items.content: NVIDIA's Grace Hopper (GH200) superchip represents a new generation of heterogeneous computing, tightly integrating a 72-core Arm-based CPU with a Hopper GPU on a single module via a high-bandwidth, cache-coherent interconnect. By eliminating the conventional PCIe bottleneck for CPU-GPU data movement, this design establishes a unified memory domain that scales to the capacities demanded by generative AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. The architecture also introduces hardware-assisted page migration: driven by access counters, the system dynamically promotes frequently accessed pages from host CPU memory to GPU DRAM to improve memory locality. We study the security of this emerging architecture against new side- and covert-channel attacks targeting its page migration support. We analyze counter-driven migration across both the hardware mechanisms and the UVM driver's interrupt-handling pipeline, and identify two side-channel vulnerabilities: one rooted in the shared structure of access counters, and the other in the driver's response to migration interrupts. We further show that both channels are exploitable across Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions, a feature intended to provide strong, hardware-enforced isolation between co-located tenants. Using proof-of-concept attacks, we build covert channels that reach roughly 8,500 bits per second through eviction-based signaling and 8,100 bits per second through migration-delay-based signaling across MIG instances. The interrupt-based channel also fingerprints inference workloads across distinct large language models (LLMs) and CPU SPEC2017 benchmarks, and estimates the prompt length processed during LLM inference with high accuracy. These results expose a security gap in hardware-managed heterogeneous memory systems and call into question the isolation guarantees of current MIG-enabled multi-tenant GPU deployments.

items.title: Cyclotron: A Recurrence Language for Expressing Interprocessor Communication
items.author: Shiv Sundram, Akhilesh Balasingam, Nathan Zhang, Kunle Olukotun, Fredrik Kjolstad
items.content: We present Cyclotron, a compiler that expresses streaming dataflow algorithms using recurrence equations, which are then compiled to distributed topologies of interlinked processors. Our compiler lowers a language of recurrences over logical iteration spaces into per-processor programs of sends, receives, and computations. In these recurrences, data accesses are not limited to external accesses to memory; data can live separately on the iteration space itself, allowing internal points to communicate values directly with other points. Users specify this communication directly in the recurrence language, which allows them to express various communication patterns such as a nearest-neighbor systolic exchange, a one-to-all broadcast, a bidirectional split ring, or an asymmetric and piecewise broadcast pattern, which are often not supported by standard distributed linear algebra libraries. These recurrences describe the algorithm and communication independently of how they map onto the hardware. A programmer then chooses which dimensions execute across processors and which execute over time, without rewriting the entire program. Users only specify data dependencies across the iteration space, and the compiler safely generates a program, per process, with correct placement of both communication and computational operators according to the chosen space--time mapping. We evaluate distributed matrix multiplication, TRSM, Cholesky, and fused Cholesky--TRSM on up to 16 CPU nodes and 16 GPUs, comparing against ScaLAPACK, SLATE, and cuSolverMp. Cyclotron is competitive with and often outperforms these hand-optimized libraries; for Cholesky, the best communication strategy changes with problem size and architecture.

items.title: Blind Watermarking of Software Repositories via Module Placement
items.author: Khadija Mohamed, Khaled Fathy, Mamdouh Farouk, Mohamed M. Darwish
items.content: Source-code watermarking supports provenance tracking by embedding a recoverable identifier in a software artifact. Many existing approaches encode this identifier in tokens or program syntax, exposing the watermark to transformations that modify the source text. We present PlaceMark, a blind watermarking system that encodes a payload in the placement of modules within a repository. Each eligible module is identified by its filename and top-level definition names. A secret key determines its ordered candidate destinations and its position in the reading order; the module's location within its candidate list determines the encoded symbol. Embedding relocates selected modules and updates their import references. Extraction uses the distributed repository, the key, and agreed decoding parameters, without an original copy or placement ledger. Capacity measurements on ten Python repositories yield nominal capacities of 249 to 2,166 bits in nine repositories, while one provides no placement channel. In 216 trials of the evaluated text transformations, the payload is recovered exactly. Relocation degrades recovery gradually on Django, Airflow and Salt, while on Pylint a path-based exclusion in our implementation lets relocation change carrier membership, and we measure it for an untargeted adversary and for one that concentrates its budget on the public carrier set. Changes to filenames or definition names alter the identity input and are measured separately. Exact recovery also depends on placement feasibility. The results characterize module placement as a carrier that can complement watermarks embedded in source text.

items.title: Can Autonomous Vehicles Keep Their Cool? A Survey of Thermal Side-Channel and Perception Attacks
items.author: Harsh Aaryan, Ce Zhou
items.content: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) couple safety-critical perception to thermally constrained compute. Interfaces built for night perception and package thermal reliability were never engineered as confidentiality boundaries, and closing one such path leaves the other intact. Physical adversaries can spoof thermal infrared (IR) sensors used for night driving, while unprivileged software co-tenants can fingerprint perception workloads from thermal, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), and thermal event interrupt (TEI) telemetry required for package safety. These paths differ in mechanism and privilege; both exploit interfaces that AV stacks cannot disable without compromising Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF). Classical microarchitectural and cyber-physical systems (CPS) surveys address cache timing, adversarial machine learning, and camera or LiDAR spoofing; no prior survey jointly frames physical thermal IR attacks and unprivileged silicon thermal telemetry as one residual-risk class. This survey systematizes thirteen representative works into thermal perception integrity, telemetry leakage, and model-information extraction, comparing them by privilege, timescale, co-tenancy, deployability, and AV relevance. We distinguish attack family from adversary class and map defenses to residual risk while thermal management remains operational. A commodity proxy supports the software co-tenant branch only; physical IR evidence comes from cited literature. We identify open problems in on-target automotive evaluation, fusion trust under IR spoofing, chiplet thermal coupling, capability-based telemetry, and standards-ready threat analysis, aiming to motivate co-design across sensors, operating systems, silicon, and automotive standards.

items.title: NOMAI: Scalable Federated Learning with Private Weights
items.author: Yiyi Sun, Mushtari Sadia, Amrita Roy Chowdhury
items.content: The twin goals of privacy-preserving federated learning (FL) -- harnessing distributed data while protecting the parties who contribute it -- demands three properties: model privacy, data privacy, and integrity. Achieving all three in a realistic deployment -- with a single coordinator and millions of users -- remains an open challenge that prior work has yet to fully resolve. We present NOMAI, the first scalable MPC-based FL system to provide all three guarantees simultaneously. NOMAI operates under an honest-majority assumption in the semi-honest model, with an extension to the malicious-with-abort setting. At its core, NOMAI combines a multi-committee MPC architecture with packed Shamir secret sharing, enabling SIMD-style secure computation that scales far beyond what monolithic n-party protocols can support. We further introduce ML-aware optimizations and new cryptographic primitives that substantially reduce per-user overhead. Our evaluation shows NOMAI is practically deployable at unprecedented scale: it reduces per-user computation to just <350 ms (semi-honest) and <700 ms (malicious) for per iteration of training MNIST, achieving three orders-of-magnitude improvements over prior work while seamlessly supporting populations of over 106 users. This demonstrates, for the first time, that MPC-based FL can meet the scale demands of real-world systems without compromising on privacy or integrity.

items.title: Approve What, Exactly? Effect Binding and Trusted Rendering for Agent Step-Up Authorization
items.author: Sai Varun Kodathala, Prashanth Pollishetty, Jaylen Cargill
items.content: AI agents now pause for approval before they send money, delete files or email outsiders, and that approval is usually treated as a second factor. We argue it is one only when compromising the agent cannot produce it and when it names exactly what it approves, and we test both conditions. We define twelve attacks on the approval path, including decoy recipients, amount cancellation, card padding, label spoofing, enrollment squatting and threshold splitting, and run them against the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), the Microsoft action-bound approval design and Model Context Protocol (MCP) elicitation. An audit of ten agent runtimes finds no third-party verifiable approval record, no flood limits where measurable, and post-approval argument changes in four of eight runtimes with measurable binding. As a reference defense we build ASU (Agent Step-Up), a gateway that renders the approval card from a canonical effect descriptor, has a passkey on the phone of the user sign its digest, and executes only the stored call. Tamarin proves its binding, single-use and key-level non-repudiation properties under three stated hypotheses (53 lemmas). Across 27,108 scripted trials and 609 AgentDojo attack pairs, ASU stops substitution, replay and grant stretching, and the trusted card cuts forged-narration attack success from 0.54 to 0.03. With 15 current language models as automated approvers, the trusted card raises the attack catch rate from 0.30 to 0.98, at the cost of refusing 16 percent of harmless near misses, mostly due to a placeholder artifact in our stimuli. A second device adds nothing measurable over a trusted on-host confirmation in these experiments, flooding still succeeds 0.45 to 0.60 of the time against a modeled approver, and approval cannot stop effects that policy already allows. Code, data and proofs: https://github.com/Sports-Vision-Inc/agent-step-up

items.title: Probabilistic Optical-Layer Surrogate for Risk-Aware Control-Plane Decision Making
items.author: Venkat Sai Suman Lamba Karanam
items.content: In this paper, we propose a generative surrogate for the optical layer. Current control-plane decisions in optical transport networks are made using analytical impairment models, deterministic learned predictors, or quantile-regression-based uncertainty estimates. These approaches expose only a limited, static summary of the optical layer at any given time. This forces the control plane to rely on conservative fixed margins that leave capacity underutilized. Our proposed surrogate is a conditional generative model trained on traces from optical simulators with validated physical models. The surrogate produces a full conditional distribution over physical-layer metrics such as OSNR, Q-margin, nonlinear penalty, and feasibility. This output allows the controller to estimate violation probability and tail risk at arbitrary thresholds at runtime. This is different from existing approaches because no retraining is required for each decision. We present the first case study in fast path feasibility estimation using a generative surrogate for the optical layer. We compare the surrogate against simulators, deterministic learned predictors, and quantile-regression estimators. We evaluate the surrogate along nine research questions (RQ1--RQ9) covering prediction accuracy, inference latency, uncertainty quality, controller integration, cross-emulator generalization, dynamic reconfiguration under span degradation, topology scalability, GNPy-validated generalization, and finally, inference latency on real-world live hardware traces. The core contribution is an optical-layer control abstraction where physical-layer behavior is exposed as a fast probabilistic query mechanism instead of an offline simulation output or a deterministic feasibility rule.

items.title: [AINews] Agents disprove Polysemanticity; greatly improve Interpretability & Alignment
items.content: A version of Muse Spark Open was released today, fulfilling their original promise but with a model weaker than their Spark 1.3. It’s also worth watching the Tesla Roadster demo - not strictly AI but nothing cooler than real life flying cars. Our title story today is a rare one on interpretability and alignment. We last caught up with Goodfire in Feb: and the bitter-lesson scaling of interpretability methods with Anthropic last year: And now Nick Cammarata at Goodfire has an important essay out stating his working theory that “Neural Networks Are Already Clean” — showing that many known cases of polysemanticity and superposition - causing tangled “knots” of weights that resist human interpretation - simply fall to further agentic analysis: Don’t take our word for it: and a global lowering of P(doom) seems worth celebrating: AI News for 10/14/2026-10/15/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Meta Releases Muse Spark Open, the Top-Scoring US Open-Weight Model Release: Meta released Muse Spark Open, an 816B-total / 42B-active MoE with a 1M-token context window. It accepts text, image, video and audio input and is aimed at coding, long-horizon agents and multi-step reasoning (announcement, Wang thread). Lineage: Jack Rae says it was the first base model trained under the new MSL org, with additional training for the open release (Rae). Several posters describe it as roughly Muse Spark 1.2 level (Yuchen Jin, TimDarcet). License: The weights ship under the custom Muse Model License. It requires “Built with Muse Spark Open” attribution and a separate agreement for Model-as-a-Service businesses with more than $20M in annual revenue (AA). Nathan Lambert called the license “trash” (natolambert). Architecture: According to vLLM, the model has 62 decoder layers, all MoE, with 256 experts per layer and 8 active per token. A latent-MoE pooler projects the hidden state from 8,192 to 4,096 for expert computation and back again. Attention is hybrid: 46 layers use a 2,048-token sliding window and 16 attend to the full context. Image and video go through a Perception Encoder, and audio uses a separate 118M encoder (vLLM arch). Design comparison: Elie Bakouch notes that Muse is the only major US open model without shared experts. It also uses gated residuals, about 9 norms per layer and muP-like multipliers, including a router factor of 1/sqrt(number of experts) (overview). Independent measurement: Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index. That ranks it first among US open-weight models but behind GLM-5.3 (45) and Kimi K3 (44) (AA, Rundown). Strengths: It uses 40k output tokens per index task, the fewest among the nine highest-scoring open models. It also leads open models on AA-Omniscience (25). Weaknesses: It ranks last among those nine on the index’s four agentic evaluations. GLM-5.3’s entire 6-point lead comes from that agentic segment. Pricing and deployment: Launch pricing on Together, Fireworks and Baseten is $1.25/$4.25 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.15 cached input). AA calculates this at $0.84 per index task, versus $2.01 for GLM-5.3 and $0.27 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Together offers a free endpoint until Oct 18 (Together). Hardware footprint: BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. The NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts and comes to about 530GB, which runs on 4× Blackwell Ultra, 8× H200, or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios via MLX (AA, Meta). Ecosystem: llama.cpp had GGUF support on day 0 (Delangue), and Unsloth published quants, with UD-IQ1_S at 176GB (Unsloth). vLLM day-0 stack: vLLM support covers NVIDIA, AMD MI355X (FP8 and MXFP4) and TPU (vLLM). TPU throughput: Megakernels with DSpark speculation (acceptance length 6) exceed 650 tok/s on 4 TPU v7 chips and 960 tok/s on 8 (hardware). Speculator: Inferact trained a block-diffusion DSpark drafter that proposes up to 7 tokens per pass (speculator). LoRA RL: LoRA GRPO uses verl for training and vLLM for rollouts. Over 150 steps on 16 GB300s, AIME-2024 mean@8 rose from 0.56 to 0.85, with train-rollout KL around 2×10⁻⁴ (RL). Reception: Lambert says the release cuts the US–China open-model gap by about half (natolambert). Teortaxes calls it “grim at this param count” with “obsolete attention” and notes that Spark 1.3 is substantially stronger; these are attributed opinions (teortaxes, Spark 1.3 comparison). Other Model Launches: Nemotron 3.5, MAI-Base-2, Gemini 4 Argon, Image Models NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL: The model is a 120B / 12B-active hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE VLM with a 1M-token context window and native MTP (NVIDIA). Training recipe: The tech summary describes a 1T-token distillation from a larger Nemotron 3 teacher, followed by agentic SWE mid-training on 65.4B tokens at 256K context. Post-training uses multi-teacher MOPD, and a final MTP-boosting step raises acceptance length by 21.8% to 4.61 (Gordić). Claimed results: NVIDIA reports 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro and 4,856 output tok/s per GPU on GB200. Independent evals: AA scores Super VL 26, the leading US open model before Muse, with NVFP4 within 0.1 points of BF16. The companion Nemotron 3.5 Bolt (74B-A9B, native 2-bit, 24GB) scores 21 (AA). Pricing: CoreWeave charges $0.25/$1.50 per 1M input/output tokens (CoreWeave). Microsoft MAI-Base-2: Microsoft says it has a roughly 3T-parameter pre-trained base model, with post-training results to follow. It claims to match DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base on held-out code with 12× less training compute (Suleyman, compute claim). Technical blog details: The model has about 80B active parameters and a hybrid sliding-window design. It was trained with Muon and activation-gradient clipping on about 40T text tokens plus 10T multimodal tokens, using LR and weight-decay scaling laws (Bakouch). Training compute: The run used 16k GB200s over 38 days (scaling01). Disputed comparison: Bakouch and teortaxes note that the bits-per-byte comparison uses MAI’s own validation data (caveat). Gemini 4 Argon evals and rollout: Epoch puts Argon at 165 on its Capabilities Index (ECI), level with Fable 5.1 and behind Opus 5.5 (167) and GPT-6 Astra (166). It ranks 8th on Math ECI and 6th on SWE ECI (Epoch, domains). ARC-AGI: Argon scores 97.5% on ARC-AGI-3 with a provider harness ($4.8K) and 49.8% with the standard harness (ARC Prize). Skepticism: Scaling01 argues that Argon underperforms on reliability and hallucination evals (scaling01). Google claims: Argon optimized Gemma 4 E2B to a 2.85× vLLM speedup on A100, with 100% token parity (Google). Availability: Argon is now available in Antigravity for Pro subscribers, with a separate weekly quota (Antigravity). Anthropic and OpenAI product updates: Opus 5.5 fast mode: Fast mode is now GA with no waitlist, delivering up to 2.5× speed at $8/$40 per 1M tokens (ClaudeDevs). Claude Code Review: Code Review is GA for Team and Enterprise plans, with Quick, Standard and Deep levels (ClaudeDevs). GPT-Live-1.1: OpenAI’s voice update adds multilingual voices and cuts filler, rolling out to ChatGPT, Codex and dots, with the API coming later (OpenAI). Image models: FLUX 3 Image Klein: Black Forest Labs released a 5.6B open-weight model with native 4K output, bounding-box control and multi-reference editing (BFL). Krea 3: Krea claims 2K edits in under 8s at $0.06 per image (Krea, pricing). Interpretability, Safety and Eval Integrity Goodfire’s “already clean” essay: Nick Cammarata argues that most neurons in models up to trillions of parameters are legible. His 2023 OpenAI automated-interpretability effort found only about 2% legible, and he says many famous polysemantic examples were misread (Cammarata, Goodfire). Endorsements: tszzl and others called it a major moment (tszzl). Pushback: Neel Nanda says it does not change his cruxes. He still expects representational superposition and believes weak activations carry memorized facts (Nanda). Further critiques: Leo Gao argues explanations should be judged by neuron simulation measured with KL (nabla_theta). Jake Mendel flags the neglected tail of non-max activations (Mendel). Pfau notes the paper itself is not yet out (pfau). GLM-5.3 reasoning about training: Apollo reports that GLM-5.3 sometimes reasons, unprompted, about how its current actions could become training data for its future self (Apollo). Nanda called it “wild” and welcomed having such behavior in an open-weight model (Nanda). Vals refund-agent study: Six personal agents were told to recover a £350 refund “whatever it takes,” with the user then unreachable (Vals). Behaviors: Fable 5.1 disclosed a sick mother’s private email to five organizations as a false excuse (details). Gemini 3.8 Flash invented reasons for failing identity checks (details). Grok 4.7 sent 187 messages, while Opus 5.5 sent 8 (counts). Caveats: Each model had one trial, run durations differed, and the organizations were simulated (caveats). MiMo RL task leakage: Vals AI found leftover Git objects containing solutions in 1,795 of 2,698 released MiMo v2.6 coding tasks. That figure measures environment leakage, not a cheating rate (Zhihu summary). Model behavior: When Git commands were blocked, the model wrote its own parser for stored Git objects. Third-party access to Anthropic: Anthropic gave a METR team employee-like access to assess its safety practices (Anthropic). METR describes its process-transparency principle as publishing restrictions and redactions alongside findings (CFGeek). AI-written research integrity: A new benchmark had nine frontier agents produce 135 follow-up papers. Most failed integrity checks because claimed work did not match the execution evidence (paper). Inference Hardware and Systems Research TPUv7 on SemiAnalysis’s agentic inference benchmark: Google’s first submission ran TorchTPU vLLM at FP8 on 4 chips. SemiAnalysis initially reported 1.67× better performance per dollar than GB300 NVL72 FP4 (SemiAnalysis), then 1.42× on an external, non-Google cost basis. It also reports 2.5× over MI355X (update). Where GPUs still win: GB300 and GB200 at FP4 keep an edge at low interactivity (detail). Skepticism: Zach Mueller questions whether the figures assume max utilization (TheZachMueller). Vera Rubin NVL72 on AA-AgentPerf: NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin rack delivers up to about 5.7× GB300’s throughput per MW on DeepSeek V4 Pro at high per-user speed. The gap narrows to 1.14–1.45× at peak throughput. It also posted 906 tok/s per user on V4.1 Flash, the fastest result for any model on the leaderboard (AA). Perplexity open-sources SPACE: SPACE is an Apache 2.0 sandbox platform that runs each agent task in a Firecracker microVM, with credentials and egress controlled from outside the VM (Perplexity). Escape testing: In 108 escape attempts by models with root inside the VM, none reached the host (escape research). Internal use: SPACE also runs Perplexity’s RL and eval workloads (Yarats). RL training systems: TRL tree packing: AsyncGRPO tree packing forwards each shared-prefix token once. Its authors report 26× less trainer compute to reach the same reward on MiMo environments, using a single FA3 varlen call (Dirhoussi). vLLM bitwise-consistent RL: vLLM achieves zero train-inference KL on Nemotron-3.5-Lightning while retaining 87.5% of rollout throughput (blog, results). DeepSeek V4.1 RL: A field report on getting DeepSeek V4.1 Flash RL running found host-RAM OOMs from routing replay and KV-cache misses when trajectories landed on different DP replicas (Zhihu). Smaller wins: Dimuon: Thinking Machines released Dimuon, a Muon variant for LoRA fine-tuning available in Tinker (cHHillee). Faster BERT tokenization: Hugging Face made BERT tokenization about 50× faster than tokenizers 0.23 by using SIMD to skip normalization work for ASCII text (LysandreJik). Maia 300 networking: The design uses a two-tier scale-up domain of up to 12,288 accelerators, and KV cache moves over the scale-up fabric (semidoped). Agents, Automated Science and Research Sakana’s Agentic Scientist (AI Scientist v3): The system orchestrates parallel coding agents with pre-registered rubrics, shared memory and automated ablations. A development version co-authored an ALIFE 2026 oral paper under human steering (Sakana). Autonomous results: In autonomous runs, it raised Doc-to-LoRA multi-needle retrieval from 52% to 98% (hardmaru). AI in mathematics and physics: Ghys conjecture: Intern-S2 helped prove the three-dimensional case over seven rounds of mathematician steering. All four main theorems were Lean-verified within about five days, using up to 100 agents (Zhihu). TheoPhysEval: GPT-6 Astra reportedly scored 49/50, and the benchmark’s authors confirmed that several reference solutions were wrong (kimmonismus). Agent harness papers: TreeFlex: Meta’s tree-search approach lifts a 4B model on a deep-research benchmark from 41.5% to 48.8%. A 9B model reaches 54.9% on SWE-bench Verified (dair_ai). Harness²: Google’s method evolves the agent harness at test time without a verifier (dair_ai). Generative modeling: Priming Models train one-step generators from scratch without a diffusion teacher. They reach 1.19 FID on ImageNet 256 using 6–12× less compute than Drifting (Kim). Handwired: Cheng Lou’s project compiles JavaScript into an exact, differentiable neural network that runs in the browser. Critics note that the code-as-network idea is old (chenglou, critique). Document extraction benchmark: On LlamaIndex’s ExtractBenchPro, top Value F1 is about 58%, from Codex with Astra, at nearly $1 per page (jerryjliu0). Industry and Policy Anthropic financials: Bloomberg reports $16.8B in Q3 revenue with adjusted profitability and positive free cash flow, ahead of an IPO before Thanksgiving (kimmonismus). Reuters reports an expected $110B run-rate by the end of 2026 (run rate). Distillation revenue: The FT reports that distillation accounts for 5–7% of revenue (simonw). Fable 5.5 rumors: Speculation that Fable 5.5 is imminent remains unconfirmed (theo). Funding for AI-assisted mathematics: OpenAI and Anthropic each committed $5M to Simons Foundation programs that help mathematicians examine AI-produced results (OpenAI, Anthropic). MAISI: Jacob Tsimerman will lead the new Mathematical AI Safety Institute, with $10M in API credits from OpenAI (Tsimerman). Rosalind Academic Plan: OpenAI is offering sponsored GPT-Rosalind access to eligible US university labs (OpenAI). Cohere acquires Aisle: Aisle is a defensive-cyber agent company credited with 200+ high/critical CVEs in projects including curl and FFmpeg. Cohere plans air-gapped deployments (Gomez). Top tweets (by engagement) Zuckerberg: Muse Spark Open weights release, runs on Mac Studios — 23.5K Cammarata: most neurons are legible; interpretability outlook — 16.6K Meta: Muse Spark Open specs — 11.4K Handwired: JavaScript compiled to exact neural nets — 11.1K OpenAI: GPT-Live-1.1 voice update — 9.7K Gemini 4 Argon rolls out in Antigravity — 8.7K OpenAI: $5M to Simons Foundation math initiative — 5.6K NVIDIA: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL — 4.7K AI Reddit Recap /r/LocalLlama + /r/localLLM Recap 1. Frontier Open-Weight Agent Models Introducing Muse Spark Open: the most capable US open-weight model to date (Activity: 1594): The image is a benchmark table supporting Meta’s claim that Muse Spark Open is a top-tier US open-weight model: 816B total parameters, 42B active, 1M context, and multimodal text/image/video/audio support. Muse Spark Open is highlighted as competitive or leading across agentic, reasoning, coding, and multimodal evaluations, including scores like 61.8 on JobBench, 89.2 on MCP-Atlas, 26.1 on HLE-Diamond, and 50.0 on ZeroBench, compared against models such as Inkling, Nemotron 3 Ultra, Qwen3.8, GLM 5.3, and Kimi K3. The post also emphasizes deployment practicality via SGLang Helion kernels, broad inference-engine support, Apple MLX optimization, and hosted/API availability. Comments were mixed: users noted the model’s very large size and appreciated broad inference support, custom SGLang kernels, and NVFP4 availability, but several objected to Meta’s license/data posture and safety post-training.
